## 📋 Locality Research Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire of 1871

**Jurisdiction:** Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, United States
**Period of focus:** ca. 1855–1885 (centered on the October 8–10, 1871 fire)
**Compiled:** 2026-08-12

---

### ⚠️ The Central Research Problem: Record Loss

The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, which housed the city's official records: deeds, birth and death registers, court records (including pre-1906 naturalizations), and tax rolls. The fire killed roughly 300 people and left more than 100,000 homeless. For genealogical purposes this creates a hard before/after divide:

- **Before October 8, 1871 — most civil records are gone.** Substitute sources (below) are essential.
- **From October 1871 onward — civil registration resumed** and records are largely intact.

*Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire*

---

### 1. Federal Census Records 🟢 Indexed + Images

**The most important pre-fire source.** Federal census originals were held in Washington, D.C., not locally — they survived the fire intact.

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|--------|----------|-------|
| **1870** | Chicago families as of June 1870 | **Critical.** Places families in Chicago just 15 months before the fire. Search this first. |
| **1860** | Earlier household enumeration | Useful for establishing pre-fire family structure |
| **1880** | Post-fire recovery period | First full census after the fire; shows reconstituted households |

- **Access:** FamilySearch (free), Ancestry.com, and NARA
- **Mortality Schedules (1850–1885)** record deaths in the year preceding each census — the 1870 mortality schedule may capture fire-related deaths occurring in that census year window.

---

### 2. Vital Records (Civil Registration) 🟡 Post-Fire Only

Cook County resumed civil registration after the fire. FamilySearch holds three indexed collections — all beginning 1871:

| Collection | Records | FamilySearch ID | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cook County Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** | ~1,450,000 | 2024189 | Indexed + images |
| **Cook County Death Records, 1871–1947** | ~980,000 | 1913456 | Indexed + images |
| **Cook County Marriage Records, 1871–1920** | ~620,000 | 1756321 | Indexed + images |

- **Gap:** No FamilySearch-indexed civil vital records exist for Chicago **before** the fire. Births, marriages, and deaths before October 1871 must be reconstructed from church records, cemetery records, and newspapers.
- **Originals:** Cook County Clerk's Office, Chicago.

---

### 3. Church Records 🟡 Partial Survival — Varies by Parish

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and are the **primary substitute for pre-fire vital events**. Survival is uneven — some parishes burned with the fire; others survived because registers were stored off-site or the church itself was spared.

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925* — **~285,000 records** (collection ID 1803978), spanning both pre- and post-fire periods. Indexed + images.
- **Catholic records:** The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds surviving Catholic parish registers. Contact them directly for pre-fire parishes. Website: https://www.archchicago.org/archives
- **Protestant and other denominations:** Check individual denominational archives. The Newberry Library holds guides to Chicago church record locations.
- **Quirk:** Always verify whether a specific parish register survived before concluding a person isn't recorded. Absence of a record may mean the register was destroyed, not that the event didn't happen.

---

### 4. Property & Land Records — Substitute Strategy 🔴 Pre-Fire Destroyed / 🟡 Post-Fire Partially Indexed

Pre-fire deeds were held in the Cook County Courthouse and were destroyed. Two substitute strategies:

**A. Burnt Record Act Reconstitutions (1872)**
Illinois's *Burnt Record Act* required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire. FamilySearch has digitized **post-fire property re-recordings**:
- Volume **009982111** — *Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880*, **112 images**, **41% name-indexed** (record-searchable) — partially browse-only for unindexed images.

**B. Pre-Fire Reconstructed Court Records**
- Volume **009982110** — *Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871*, **38 images**, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image-by-image with no search capability.

**C. Chicago Title and Trust Company Records**
Insurance and title company records became vital substitutes for pre-fire property ownership. The **Chicago History Museum** holds the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection. *(Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)*

- **Federal land patents** (original land grants prior to private ownership) were held federally and survived — search the BLM General Land Office Records at https://glorecords.blm.gov/

---

### 5. City Directories 🟢 Survived — Physical/Microfilm

City directories are among the most valuable pre-fire substitutes. Published commercially and distributed widely, they were not held in the courthouse and largely survived. The **Newberry Library** holds Chicago city directories from the **1840s onward**.

- Name, occupation, and street address for heads of household
- Especially valuable for 1860s–early 1870s to place families before the fire
- The Newberry Library, 60 West Walnut Street, Chicago — https://www.newberry.org

---

### 6. Newspapers 🟢 Indexed + Images (Subscription)

Chicago newspapers published **lists of the dead, missing, and displaced** in the days and weeks after the fire — a direct genealogical substitute when civil records are absent.

- **Chicago Tribune** (1847–present): Covered the fire extensively; obituaries and survivor notices
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) — subscription; also ProQuest Historical Newspapers
- **Chicago History Museum** holds additional newspaper holdings and personal papers of fire survivors

---

### 7. Military Records 🟢 Indexed (Federal Holdings — Survived Fire)

Many Chicago men served in the Civil War (1861–1865). Federal military records were held in Washington and were unaffected by the fire.

- **Service & Pension Records:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) — https://www.archives.gov; also Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) for digitized service records
- **Illinois Adjutant General Records:** Illinois State Archives, Springfield — rosters of Illinois regiments
- **Grand Army of the Republic (GAR):** Post records for Cook County veterans may be at the Illinois State Archives or Chicago History Museum

---

### 8. Immigration & Naturalization Records 🔴 Pre-Fire Destroyed / 🟢 Post-Fire and Federal Holdings Intact

- **Pre-1871 naturalizations** were held in local courts and were destroyed. The only recourse is to look for duplicate filings in federal courts (which were separate from the county courthouse).
- **Passenger lists (ship manifests):** Held at NARA — unaffected by the fire. Search via FamilySearch, Ancestry.com, or directly at NARA. Chicago was not a port of entry; most immigrant ancestors arrived via New York, Baltimore, or New Orleans and traveled overland.
- **Post-1871 naturalizations:** Filed in Cook County Circuit Court — held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** can appear in any court of record (federal, state, or local). After September 26, 1906, USCIS (then Bureau of Naturalization) centralized records.

---

### 9. Probate Records 🔴 Pre-Fire Destroyed / 🟡 Post-Fire

- Pre-fire probate files were in the Cook County Courthouse — destroyed.
- Post-fire probate records (1871+): **IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University** (Cook County Circuit Court records). Contact: https://library.neiu.edu/irad
- The Chicago History Museum may hold transcripts or abstracts of some pre-fire estate proceedings.

---

### 10. Cemetery & Burial Records 🟢 Partially Indexed

- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com): The most comprehensive online cemetery index; many Chicago-area cemeteries are indexed, including Graceland, Rosehill, and Oak Woods — all of which received fire victims
- **Chicago History Museum** holds burial permit records and sexton's logs for some cemeteries

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Strengths | URL / Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Post-fire vital records, church records, census, military | familysearch.org |
| **Newberry Library** | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, published genealogies | newberry.org |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Insurance/title records, fire survivor papers, newspapers, photographs | chicagohistory.org |
| **IRAD-NEIU** | Post-fire Cook County court, naturalization, probate records | library.neiu.edu/irad |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | archchicago.org/archives |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871+ (originals) | cookcountyclerk.com |
| **Illinois State Archives** | State-level records, military rosters | ilsos.gov/departments/archives |
| **NARA (Great Lakes Region)** | Federal census originals, naturalization, military, immigration | archives.gov |

---

### Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Pre-fire civil records (before October 8, 1871) are largely gone** — do not expect to find birth, death, marriage, or deed records in a courthouse repository for that period. Build your pre-fire picture from the 1870 census, church records, city directories, and newspapers first.
2. **The 1870 federal census survived** because originals were held in Washington, D.C. — this is your single most important source for placing a family in Chicago just before the fire.
3. **Absence of a pre-fire church register entry may mean the register was destroyed**, not that the event didn't occur — always verify the survival status of a specific parish's records before drawing a negative conclusion.
4. **The Burnt Record Act (1872) re-recordings are a direct substitute for pre-fire deeds** — search these before concluding a property transaction can't be documented.
5. **FamilySearch's two digitized volumes for this period** (pre-fire reconstructed court records 1865–1871 and post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880) must be partially browsed image-by-image — 0% of the first and ~59% of the second are not name-indexed.
6. **External links returned by FamilySearch for this time window are generic** (Ancestry census, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — no fire-specific curated link set exists; go directly to the Chicago History Museum and Newberry Library for the most targeted pre-fire substitute sources.

---

### Suggested Search Order for Fire-Affected Families

1. **1870 federal census** — establish the household before the fire
2. **FamilySearch church records collection** (ID 1803978) — find baptisms, marriages, burials pre-fire

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

**French Louisiana** (*La Louisiane*) was an administrative district of New France. France controlled the territory from 1682 to 1762. Key facts directly relevant to record creation:

- New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville — the earliest parish registers date from that same year
- The **Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church** in French Louisiana — it was the sole record-keeping authority for vital events
- The **Code Noir** required Catholic baptism of every enslaved person, generating a distinctive and genealogically important record class
- France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); the eastern strip went to Britain
- Spain administered the colony 1762–1800, then briefly retroceded it to France before the Louisiana Purchase (1803)

> ⚠️ **Critical jurisdictional warning for the 1700s**: Louisiana passed through *three sovereign administrations* within a single century — French (to 1762), Spanish (1762–1800), briefly French again (1800–1803). A family active across that century will have records in two entirely different legal and administrative systems. Search both French and Spanish colonial record series for families straddling 1762.

Population data for the French colonial period is not available from FamilySearch's database. The European and African colonial population grew from a few thousand in the early 1700s to tens of thousands by mid-century.

---

## Boundary Changes / Jurisdictional Succession

| Period | Sovereign | Administrative Body | Record Custodian |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1699–1762 | France | Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur), New Orleans | Louisiana Historical Center; ANOM (France) |
| 1762–1800 | Spain | Cabildo (Spanish colonial council) | Louisiana Historical Center; Archivo General de Indias (Spain) |
| 1800–1803 | France (briefly) | — | Transitional |
| 1803+ | United States | U.S. territorial/state government | NARA; Louisiana State Archives |

Records created during the French period (pre-1762) are ultimately under the custody of French colonial archives. For families active before *and* after 1762, continue into the Spanish Cabildo and Spanish notarial records — do not stop at the 1762 transfer date.

---

## Available Record Types

### ⭐ Church Records — PRIMARY SOURCE FOR THE ENTIRE PERIOD

The Catholic Church was the sole legal authority for vital registration in French Louisiana, making sacramental registers the single most important record class for 1700s research.

- **Record types**: Baptisms (*baptêmes*), marriages (*mariages*), burials (*sépultures*)
- **Special class**: The Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons — enslaved individuals appear in registers, often with both an African name and a baptismal name alongside the enslaver's name. These registers are frequently the *only* documentary trace for enslaved ancestors in this era.
- **Earliest registers**: St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans — from **1720** *(source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*
- **FamilySearch digitized collection**: [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) (Collection ID 1612905) — **987,654 indexed records; 493,827 images** — **Indexed + Images** — coverage begins 1718, spanning the entire French colonial period
- **Language**: ⚠️ **18th-century French** (sacramental formulas sometimes in Latin). Researchers must be able to read French colonial cursive script.
- **Where held**: St. Louis Cathedral Archives (New Orleans); Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans); FamilySearch (digitized)

---

### ⭐ Superior Council Records — KEY CIVIL/LEGAL SOURCE

The *Conseil Supérieur* was the chief governing and judicial body of French Louisiana. Its records are a major source for civil genealogical data.

- **Record types**: Land grants (*concessions*), court proceedings, commercial contracts, estate inventories, civil and criminal cases — all of which name individuals and their family relationships
- **Date range**: French colonial period (1700s) through 1762; succeeded by the Spanish Cabildo after 1762
- **Where held**: **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized *(source: [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*
- **Digitization level**: Partially digitized — physical access required for many items; check the Louisiana Historical Center's online catalog before visiting
- **Language**: ⚠️ French; requires knowledge of colonial French administrative terminology

---

### ⭐ Notarial Records — ESSENTIAL CIVIL SOURCE FROM 1730s

The New Orleans Notarial Archives is the **oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America**.

- **Record types**: Contracts, wills (*testaments*), marriage settlements (*contrats de mariage*), property sales and transfers, estate inventories — often naming multiple family members and relationships not recorded elsewhere
- **Date range**: From the **1730s** onward *(source: [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))*
- **Where held**: New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — provides public access
- **Digitization level**: Physical repository access required for most colonial-era volumes; some finding aids available online
- **Language**: ⚠️ French (later Spanish for the 1762–1800 period)

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **No civil vital registration existed in Louisiana during the 1700s.** The Catholic Church was the effective registration authority.
- Statewide civil registration did not begin until the 20th century.
- Catholic parish registers (above) are the sole systematic alternative.

---

### Land Records

- Louisiana followed **civil law land grant traditions** (not English common law), reflecting its French colonial heritage
- **French concessions** (grants to settlers) were made by the colonial government
- **Where documented**: American State Papers: Public Lands series; Louisiana State Land Office *(source: [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))*
- **Language**: ⚠️ French

---

### Probate and Estate Records

- **FamilySearch collection**: [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) (Collection ID 2078341) — **456,789 indexed records; 228,394 images** — **Indexed + Images** — coverage begins **1756**, overlapping the late French colonial period
- Colonial-era estate records also appear within the Superior Council records (pre-1762)
- ⚠️ Louisiana probate follows **civil law** (not English common law inheritance) — estate records are structured differently from those in other U.S. states, but are often *more* detailed

---

### Census and Population Records

- The French colonial administration conducted periodic population rolls of the colony
- **Where held**: **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — colonial census rolls and administrative correspondence *(source: [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*
- **Digitization level**: ANOM has digitized a significant portion of its holdings; accessible via [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](http://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)
- U.S. federal censuses begin only in 1790 (post-colonial for most of the 1700s); the first Louisiana federal census was 1810

---

### Military Records

- French colonial militia musters and military correspondence exist for the 1700s
- **Where held**: Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence — primary custodian for French colonial military records
- NARA holds some records transferred at the Louisiana Purchase
- [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) has some early Louisiana military records, but coverage for the French colonial period is limited
- **Digitization level**: Primarily held at ANOM (partially digitized); no specific FamilySearch-indexed collection for 1700s Louisiana military records

---

### Immigration and Ethnic Origins

- French colonists came primarily from France (Paris basin, Loire Valley, coastal provinces) and French Canada
- Enslaved Africans were imported, primarily from Senegambia in the early colonial period
- German settlers populated the *Côte des Allemands* (German Coast) north of New Orleans from the 1720s
- **Where to research origins**: ANOM holds passenger and colonist lists for French Louisiana; French national archives (Paris) hold supplementary emigration records
- No FamilySearch-indexed passenger list collection exists specifically for French colonial Louisiana arrivals

---

### Cemetery Records

- Colonial burials were in Catholic churchyard cemeteries; burial entries are part of the parish registers (see Church Records above)
- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) includes some colonial-era burials, but coverage for 18th-century Louisiana is sparse
- Physical cemetery or Catholic archive access is the most reliable source for this period

---

### Newspapers

- No newspapers existed in Louisiana during the French colonial period
- Louisiana's first newspaper (*Le Moniteur de la Louisiane*) was not established until 1794 — during the Spanish period
- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) has no Louisiana content for the French colonial period

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for French Colonial Louisiana | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — 987,654 records, images (indexed); [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — 456,789 records, images (indexed) | Free |
| **ANOM** (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer) | Colonial administrative records, census rolls, military correspondence | Free (online portal) |
| **NARA** (National Archives) | Some colonial-era records transferred at the Louisiana Purchase | Free / in-person |
| **Ancestry.com** | Some Louisiana records; 1700s colonial coverage is limited | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Some early Louisiana military records | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records (partially digitized); colonial-era documents | In-person |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from 1730s (contracts, wills, marriage settlements) | In-person; some online catalog |
| **St. Louis Cathedral Archives**, New Orleans | Parish registers from 1720 | Contact parish |
| **Louisiana State Archives**, Baton Rouge | State-era records; some colonial-era holdings | In-person / online request |
| **Louisiana State Land Office**, Baton Rouge | French concessions, land grant records | In-person / online |
| **ANOM**, Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence, census rolls, military records for French colonial period | In-person / online portal |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following exist but are **not fully available in any online database**:
- **Superior Council court proceedings** (partially digitized at Louisiana Historical Center; most require in-person access)
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives colonial-era acts** (physical access required for most 18th-century volumes)
- **French colonial census rolls** (primarily at ANOM; partially available via their online portal)
- **French colonial militia/military records** (primarily at ANOM)
- **Parish registers outside New Orleans** (coverage varies; some digitized on FamilySearch, others physical only)

---

## Known Record Losses

- Louisiana's colonial record survival is **relatively good** because the Catholic Church maintained registers independently of the civil government, creating redundancy
- The **New Orleans fires of 1788 and 1794** destroyed portions of the city, but many church and notarial records survived due to dispersed storage
- **Hurricane and flood damage** over the centuries has affected some archival holdings at local institutions
- **The 1762 French-to-Spanish transfer** did not cause wholesale record destruction; Spanish authorities maintained and continued French records, preserving continuity
- Gaps exist in coverage for smaller outlying settlements beyond New Orleans

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with FamilySearch's Church Records collection.** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) is indexed, has images, and covers the entire French colonial period. It is the fastest entry point.

2. **Records are in 18th-century French.** All French colonial Louisiana records require reading cursive French from the 1700s (and sometimes Latin). Plan for translation. Spanish-period records (1762–1800) are in Spanish.

3. **Follow families across the 1762 sovereignty change.** A family active before and after 1762 will have records in both the French Superior Council system and the Spanish Cabildo/notarial system. Do not stop research at the political boundary.

4. **Consult ANOM for French origins.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence is the primary repository for identifying where colonial-era Louisiana ancestors originated in France. Their online portal makes remote access possible before planning a physical visit.

5. **The New Orleans Notarial Archives are a genealogical goldmine.** Marriage contracts and estate inventories from the 1730s onward name family members and relationships that appear nowhere else. In-person or researcher-assisted access is required.

6. **Use Code Noir records strategically for enslaved ancestors.** Enslaved persons baptized under the Code Noir appear in Catholic registers — often the only documentary trace for African-descended ancestors in this period. The FamilySearch Church Records collection indexes these entries alongside free persons.

7. **Louisiana's civil law tradition differs from other U.S. states.** Probate and property records follow French/Spanish civil law (community property, forced heirship) — estates were often documented more comprehensively than in common-law states.

8. **Use the FamilySearch Wiki** for updated collection pointers: [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records) and [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).

9. **For late-period colonial probate (1756+)**, the FamilySearch [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) is indexed with images — a significant convenience for colonial-era research.

---

> **Coverage note:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana-specific research pages did not return dedicated content for this jurisdiction from the wiki tool; the Louisiana-specific guidance above is grounded in two wiki search results ([Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records) and [Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)) and the Wikipedia article on [French Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana). Consult those pages directly for the most current detail.

# Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide
**Time Period: Late 1800s (c. 1870–1906) | Compiled 2026-08-12**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania's coal mining world divides into two distinct geographic regions, each with its own counties and record repositories:

**Anthracite (Hard Coal) Region — Northeastern PA:**
The core counties — Schuylkill (formed 1811), Luzerne, Carbon (formed 1843), Northumberland, and Lackawanna (formed from Luzerne County in 1878) — were the center of the global anthracite trade. Major towns include Pottsville, Wilkes-Barre, Scranton, Mauch Chunk (now Jim Thorpe), and Shamokin.

**Bituminous (Soft Coal) Region — Western PA:**
Westmoreland (formed 1773), Fayette, Washington, and Allegheny counties. Different immigrant communities (more German and eastern European) and different company structures than the anthracite region.

> ⚠️ **Critical boundary quirk:** Lackawanna County (Scranton, Carbondale) did not exist until 1878 — it was carved from Luzerne County. Records for families in that area **before 1878** are filed under **Luzerne County**. Always search Luzerne first for Scranton-area families in the 1870s and earlier.

---

## Vital Records

**Pennsylvania had no statewide civil birth or death registration before 1906.** A registration law existed 1852–1855 but was poorly enforced and compliance was minimal. For the entire late 1800s target window, church records are your primary substitute for vital events.

| Record | Date Range | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| PA Death Certificates | 1906–1968 | FamilySearch [coll. 2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) | **Indexed + images** (4.2M records) |
| County Marriages | 1885–1950 | FamilySearch [coll. 1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | **Indexed + images** (524K records) |
| Civil Marriages | 1677–1950 | FamilySearch [coll. 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | **Indexed + images** (312K records) |
| Compiled Marriages | 1700–1900 | FamilySearch [coll. 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | **Index only — no images** |

> ⚠️ Death certificates begin in 1906, just after the target window. For deaths in the late 1800s, look to church burial registers, cemetery records, Mine Inspector reports, and newspaper notices.

---

## Church Records ⭐ — The Single Most Important Source for This Period

Ethnic parishes were the backbone of mining community life, and their registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are often the **only** surviving documentation of vital events before 1906. Mining towns typically had multiple churches organized by national origin:

| Ethnicity | Denominations |
|---|---|
| Irish | Catholic (e.g., St. Patrick's parishes) |
| Welsh | Congregational, Presbyterian, Baptist |
| German | Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic |
| Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian | Catholic (separate national parishes, often 1880s–1890s) |
| Ukrainian, Rusyn | Greek Catholic, Orthodox |
| Italian | Catholic |

**On FamilySearch:** [Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) — 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons, 607,220 images — **indexed + images**, covers the full target window.

**Other repositories:** Many parish registers remain with individual churches or at diocesan archives:
- **Diocese of Scranton** — covers Lackawanna, Luzerne, and surrounding counties
- **Diocese of Allentown** — covers Schuylkill, Carbon, and surrounding counties
- Welsh Congregational and Presbyterian records at denominational archives (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)

---

## Census Records

| Census | Notes |
|---|---|
| 1870 Federal | Lists occupation ("miner", "laborer in mine") — key for identifying mining families |
| 1880 Federal | More detailed — lists relationship to head, birthplace of parents |
| 1890 Federal | **Largely destroyed by fire** — a critical gap |
| 1900 Federal | Includes years of immigration, citizenship status, number of children |
| Mortality Schedules 1870, 1880 | List deaths in the year preceding the census with cause — valuable for pre-1906 deaths |

Pennsylvania did not conduct state censuses during this period. The 1890 gap is especially painful for coal-region research — church records, city directories, and tax lists become essential substitutes for that decade.

---

## Occupational & Mining-Specific Records ⭐

These are the records that set coal-region research apart from standard genealogy:

### State Mine Inspector Reports (1870–onward)
Published **annually** starting 1870, these reports list every **fatal accident** with the miner's name, age, nationality, and cause of death. They are among the most genealogically rich occupational records in American history and are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). Some years are digitized; check the Archives' online catalog.
> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)

### Digitized Mining Volumes on FamilySearch

| Volume | County | Date Range | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mine Worker Employment Cards (IGN 002240015) | Schuylkill | 1870–1900 | 410 | **Indexed + full-text searchable** (95% name-indexed) |
| Mine Accident Reports (IGN 002240016) | Luzerne | 1870–1895 | 287 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — must be viewed image-by-image, no name index |
| Colliery Payroll Ledgers (IGN 002240017) | Lackawanna | 1878–1900 | 199 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — must be viewed image-by-image, no name index |

> Note: The Luzerne Mine Accident Reports and Lackawanna Colliery Payroll Ledgers are not indexed and not full-text searchable. You must browse all images manually. These are particularly valuable if you know roughly when and where an ancestor worked.

### Company & Employment Records
Employment records (payrolls, accident reports, company store ledgers) survive **fragmentarily** at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties. Coverage is uneven — not all companies kept records, and many were lost.
> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)

### Union Records
The **United Mine Workers of America (UMWA)**, founded 1890, created membership rolls, grievance files, and meeting minutes. These are primarily held at the UMWA archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives. For the earlier period (1860s–1870s), **Molly Maguires** trial records name many Schuylkill County miners and may be a source for that community.

---

## Immigration & Naturalization Records ⭐

Immigration is **essential** for coal-region research — the vast majority of miners in the late 1800s were immigrants or children of immigrants:

- **Early waves (1840s–1860s):** Irish, Welsh, English, German
- **Later waves (1880s–1900s):** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Czech, Italian, Ukrainian, Rusyn

**Where to look:**

| Record | Repository | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Passenger arrival lists | NARA (Philadelphia & New York ports) / Ancestry / FamilySearch | Philadelphia was the primary port for many Schuylkill County arrivals |
| Naturalization records | County courthouse where miner lived; Pennsylvania State Archives | Pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize — check all courts in the county |
| Schuylkill Co. naturalizations (1840s–1906) | **Pennsylvania State Archives** | Specifically noted in FamilySearch Wiki |
| Declaration of Intent ("first papers") | Same county courts | Filed separately from final naturalization; often contains birthplace detail |

> Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)

---

## Probate Records

[Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records, 446,607 images — **indexed + images** on FamilySearch. County orphans' courts hold original records; registers of wills at county courthouses.

> Note: Many miners in company towns rented company housing and owned little property — probate records may be thin or absent. Don't read a missing will as a negative — it may simply reflect the economic conditions.

---

## Military Records

Civil War veterans were common in the mining workforce of the 1870s–1890s. Check:
- **Civil War service records and pension files** at NARA (also on Ancestry and Fold3)
- **Pennsylvania adjutant general records** at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- Pension files are genealogically rich — widow's pensions especially contain marriage and family information

---

## Newspapers

Mining accidents, strikes, union activities, deaths, and social events were extensively covered in local papers. The **Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) is the flagship coal-region paper dating to 1825. Other key papers include the Scranton Tribune and Wilkes-Barre Times. Access via:
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) — good Pennsylvania coverage
- **Chronicling America** (free, Library of Congress) — some Pennsylvania coal-region papers
- **Historical societies** hold original or microfilm runs

---

## Repositories Summary

| Repository | What's There | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports, naturalization records, some company records | In person or online catalog at phmc.pa.gov |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church/town records, marriage collections, probate, mining volumes | Free online; some browsable, some indexed |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** | Local mining collections, newspapers, family files | In person (Pottsville, PA) |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton) | Mining community records, oral histories, photographs | In person; check their archive holdings |
| **County courthouses** | Deeds, naturalizations, court records, wills | In person; some on FamilySearch or Ancestry |
| **Diocesan archives** (Scranton; Allentown) | Pre-1906 Catholic parish registers | Contact each diocese for access |
| **NARA** (Philadelphia & Washington) | Passenger lists, military records, federal court records | In person, Ancestry, Fold3 |
| **Ancestry.com / FindMyPast** | Census, immigration, naturalization, newspapers | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave / BillionGraves** | Cemetery inscriptions — many coal-region cemeteries indexed | Free online |

---

## Key Research Gaps & Quirks

1. **No statewide vital registration before 1906** — church records are your birth/death source for the entire target window.
2. **1890 federal census destroyed** — substitute with 1889/1890 city directories, tax lists, church records, and company payrolls.
3. **Lackawanna County pre-1878** — search Luzerne County for all Scranton/Carbondale records before Lackawanna's formation in 1878.
4. **Luzerne and Lackawanna mining volumes are browse-only** — plan extra time to scroll through unindexed images for those counties.
5. **Ethnic parish research requires knowing the denomination** — a Polish miner would not appear in an Irish Catholic register. Identifying the ancestor's nationality and religion unlocks the right church.
6. **Company towns** — miners in patch towns (company-owned villages) may appear in company store ledgers and housing records, not just civil records. These survive only fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local societies.
7. **Molly Maguires trials (1876–1879)** — if your Schuylkill County ancestors were Irish miners of that era, court records from these celebrated trials may name individuals in your research community.

---

**Where to Start:** If you know a specific county, search the FamilySearch Church and Town Records collection first, then pull the relevant federal census years (1870, 1880, 1900). Follow with immigration/naturalization records if foreign-born, and check the Pennsylvania State Archives Mine Inspector reports for any ancestor who died in service. # Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (Early 1600s — Puritan Settlement Era, c. 1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Colonies in this period:** Two *separate* colonies coexisted: **Plymouth Colony** (founded 1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (founded 1628, settled at scale from 1630). They remained legally distinct until 1691, when they merged as the **Province of Massachusetts Bay**. Records for each colony are maintained separately and must be searched independently.
- **County formation:** The original four counties were established in **1643**: Suffolk (Boston area), Essex (northeastern coast), Middlesex (Cambridge/Concord area), and Old Norfolk (covering what is now coastal New Hampshire and northeastern Massachusetts — later dissolved). Plymouth Colony established its own county in **1685**. Before 1643, there were no counties; the **town** was the sole unit of civil government and the primary record-keeping entity throughout the entire colonial period.
- **Government:** Town meetings governed local affairs. The General Court (colonial legislature) sat as the supreme legislative and judicial authority. County courts handled probate, land, and civil/criminal matters after 1643.
- **Population:** No population figures were returned by the tool for this period. Historically, the Great Migration brought approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (per the Wikipedia article on Massachusetts Bay Colony: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony). By 1700, the colonial population was estimated at roughly 55,000–70,000.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fishing, timber, maritime trade, and small craftwork. No major industrial record series exist for this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small numbers of servants, Indigenous peoples, and (by late century) African enslaved persons appear in some records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalism was the established church of Massachusetts Bay Colony. Plymouth Colony was Separatist Congregationalist. Small numbers of Anglicans, Quakers (especially after 1650s), and Baptists also appear — all often documented through disciplinary proceedings in Congregational records.
- **Key historical events:** Pequot War (1636–1637); Anne Hutchinson's Antinomian Controversy and trial (1637–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1676) — the deadliest per-capita war in American history, generating significant militia and casualty records; King William's War (1689–1697); Salem Witch Trials (1692) — extensive court documentation survives.

---

## Boundary changes

- **Before 1643:** No county structure existed. All civil authority flowed through individual towns and the General Court. There is no "county" to search for events before 1643 — go directly to town records and the Massachusetts Archives.
- **1643:** Four original counties established (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Old Norfolk). Probate courts and county courts begin functioning.
- **1685:** Plymouth Colony formally establishes Plymouth County.
- **1691:** Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony merge as the Province of Massachusetts Bay. Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) remain a separate documentary corpus — they are **not** subsumed into the Massachusetts Bay series. Search them independently.
- **Old Norfolk County** (1643–c.1680): Covered what is now coastal southeastern New Hampshire and northeastern Massachusetts. It was dissolved and its territory redistributed. If your ancestors were in towns near the NH border (Salisbury, Haverhill, Hampton, Exeter), determine which jurisdiction — Old Norfolk or Essex — held their records.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (town-level civil registration)
- **Start date — town level:** The General Court ordered towns to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639**, making Massachusetts one of the earliest jurisdictions in North America to mandate civil registration at the town level. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Start date — statewide:** Statewide civil vital registration did not begin until **1841**. Do not conflate these two levels: the 1639 mandate is town-level; the 1841 mandate is state-level.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by town clerks. Completeness varies significantly by town and clerk. Early records may be sparse, entered after the fact, or missing for some towns entirely.
- **Published compilations:** The multi-volume **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series (known as the Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. This is a critical finding aid before going to original volumes. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (Collection ID: 2061550; 3,456,789 records, 1,728,394 images) — covers our entire target window. Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550. The tool does not report `recordSearchablePercent`; treat as potentially **indexed + images** but verify at the collection landing page.
- **Plymouth Colony vitals:** Covered separately — see Plymouth Colony records below.
- **Where held (originals):** Individual town clerk offices; Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds some original colony-era records from the 1620s.

### Church records
- **Primary denomination:** Congregational (Puritan). As the established church of Massachusetts Bay Colony, Congregational meetings kept registers of members, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary actions (excommunications, admonishments). These are essential records for the 1620–1700 period. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (Collection ID: 1921657; 987,654 records, 493,827 images) — starts in 1630, covering our period. Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657.
- **Published transcriptions:** Many early Congregational records have been published in the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** series and local historical society publications. Check NEHGS holdings.
- **Other denominations:** Quaker Monthly Meeting records survive for congregations founded after the 1650s; Baptist records are sparse for this era. Anglican (Church of England) presence was minimal until after 1686 (Dominion of New England period).
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Where held:** Local congregations (some still active), Massachusetts Archives, NEHGS, American Congregational Association (Boston).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Does not apply — the first U.S. federal census was in 1790. No federal enumerations exist for the 1620–1700 period.
- **Colonial-era substitutes:**
  - **Tax lists / rates:** The General Court periodically assessed taxes on towns; some survive at the Massachusetts Archives and have been published.
  - **Militia musters and lists:** Especially important during King Philip's War (1675–1676) — militia rolls survive at the Massachusetts Archives and have been partially published. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)
  - **Proprietors' records:** Town proprietors (original land grantees) kept lists of shareholders that can function like censuses.
  - **"Strangers" lists:** Some towns recorded non-freemen residents.
- **No colonial Massachusetts census substitute is available as an indexed FamilySearch collection** for this period — researchers must work from published tax lists, militia musters, and local histories.

### Probate records
- **Start date:** Probate jurisdiction began at the county level with the establishment of the four original counties in **1643**. Some Plymouth Colony probate activity predates that, handled by the colony's General Court.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (Collection ID: 1678901; 567,890 records, 283,945 images) — covers our target period from 1635 forward. Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901.
- **Record types:** Wills, intestate administrations, inventories of estates, guardianship records, distribution accounts. Inventories are especially valuable — they list all personal property and often reveal occupations, literacy, and household composition.
- **Where held (originals):** County probate courts (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Plymouth after 1685). The Massachusetts Archives holds colonial-era records. Many early probate records have been published and indexed.

### Land records
- **System:** Metes and bounds. Massachusetts is a state-land state — land was granted by the colonial government to towns, which then distributed parcels to individual settlers. This creates a two-tier record structure: colony/town grants AND individual deeds.
- **Start date:** County registries of deeds began recording deeds from the **1630s** and survive in "remarkably complete runs." (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)
- **Types:** Town proprietors' records (original divisions of land), deeds recorded at county registries, colony patents.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (originals); Massachusetts Archives holds colony-level grants. Some early deed books have been microfilmed by FamilySearch but no dedicated colonial-era land deed FamilySearch collection for Massachusetts was returned by the tool — treat as **physical or microfilm only** until verified.
- **Plymouth Colony:** Plymouth Colony land records are published separately.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts in period:**
  - **Pequot War (1636–1637):** Militia involvement; some muster rolls survive.
  - **King Philip's War (1675–1676):** The most destructive war of the colonial period. Militia rolls survive at the Massachusetts Archives and have been partially published. This is the primary military record source for men of this generation. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)
  - **King William's War (1689–1697):** Militia records; some published.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); partially published by historical and genealogical societies. Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some military records, though its primary Massachusetts colonial coverage is limited — verify before subscribing.
- **No pension or bounty land records** exist for the colonial militia period; those systems did not yet exist.

### Court records
- **Types:** The **General Court** (legislature/supreme court), **county courts**, and **Courts of General Sessions** all generated records documenting criminal proceedings, civil disputes, guardianships, and administrative actions. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)
- **Salem Witch Trials (1692):** Extensive court documentation survives and has been published and digitized. The Salem Witch Trials Documentary Archive (University of Virginia) is a key online resource.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds General Court records from the 1620s onward. County court records are at county repositories and the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Note:** Court records often name family members (guardians, witnesses, sureties) not found elsewhere.

### Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) — *treat as a separate research universe*
- Plymouth Colony maintained its own government, courts, and records from 1620 until the 1691 merger. These records are **published and indexed separately** from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Key publications:** *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (12 volumes, published 1855–1861) — includes court orders, deeds, probate, vital records, lists of freemen, militia lists.
- If your ancestors were in Plymouth, Duxbury, Scituate, Barnstable, Sandwich, Yarmouth, Taunton, or other Plymouth Colony towns before 1691, begin here.

### Immigration / passenger records (Great Migration era)
- **Context:** The Great Migration brought ~20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1643. Tracing their English origins requires specialized tools.
- **FamilySearch Passenger Lists collection** (ID: 1784312, 1820–1891) covers **1820–1891 only** — it does not cover colonial-era arrivals. Do not use it for 1620–1700 research.
- **Key finding aids for colonial arrivals:**
  - **Great Migration Study:** NEHGS's multi-volume series documents every known settler who arrived in New England 1620–1643, with family reconstructions and source citations. Available at NEHGS (nehgs.org) and in major genealogical libraries.
  - **Early American passengers:** Charles Banks's *Planters of the Commonwealth* (1930) and similar works list known ship passengers.
  - **Winthrop Fleet (1630):** Lists of passengers survive for some ships.
- **Where to access:** NEHGS library and online subscription (AmericanAncestors.org); published volumes in major genealogical libraries.

### Cemetery records
- **Colonial-era burials:** Many early settlers were buried in churchyard or town burying grounds. Some headstones survive; many do not, or they predate engraved stones.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage of historic Massachusetts cemeteries, including colonial-era stones. Coverage is volunteer-driven and uneven for pre-1700 graves.
- **Published transcriptions:** The Epitaphs of the Old Burying Grounds of Massachusetts and similar local compilations. NEHGS holds many cemetery transcription collections.
- **Sexton records:** For most towns, sexton records do not survive for the 1620–1700 period.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax "rates" assessed by the General Court; town rate lists. These are the closest equivalent to a census for this period.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; some published in town histories and genealogical journals.

### Newspapers
- **Not applicable for this period.** The first American newspaper (*Publick Occurrences*) was published in Boston in 1690 but suppressed after one issue. Regular newspapers in Massachusetts did not begin until 1704 (*Boston News-Letter*). Newspapers.com is not a useful resource for 1620–1700 Massachusetts research.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (3.4M records); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (987K records); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (567K records) | Free |
| **AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS)** | Great Migration Study; manuscript collections; published genealogies; colonial vital records | Subscription |
| **Massachusetts Archives Digital** | Some colonial-era documents digitized | Free / limited |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery inscriptions (partial coverage of colonial burying grounds) | Free |
| **Fold3** | Some colonial militia records | Subscription (verify coverage before purchasing) |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal records; minimal relevance for pre-1700 period | Free / fee for copies |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston, MA) | Original colony records from 1620s; General Court records; county court records; militia rolls; tax lists | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** (Boston, MA) | Largest genealogical library in New England; manuscript collections; Great Migration series; published genealogies | In-person (members); online via AmericanAncestors.org |
| **County Registries of Deeds** (Essex, Suffolk, Middlesex, Plymouth) | Deeds from 1630s onward in "remarkably complete runs" | In-person; some online via MassCourts or county websites |
| **County Probate Courts** | Colonial-era probate records (wills, inventories, administrations) | In-person; some on FamilySearch |
| **American Congregational Association / Congregational Library** (Boston, MA) | Congregational church records, ministers' records | In-person |
| **Individual town clerk offices** | Original town vital record volumes | In-person / correspondence |
| **Plymouth County Registry of Deeds / Probate** | Plymouth Colony–era records | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following exist but are not fully available in any major online database:

- **Colonial-era deeds** recorded at county registries (pre-1700): FamilySearch has not returned a dedicated indexed land record collection for this period; deed books may be on FamilySearch microfilm or accessible only in-person.
- **Town proprietors' records**: Held at individual town clerk offices or historical societies; rarely digitized.
- **Colonial tax/rate lists**: At Massachusetts Archives; some published in genealogical journals but not comprehensively searchable online.
- **General Court records** (legislative/judicial): Massachusetts Archives; not fully digitized or indexed.
- **Most local Congregational church records not in the FamilySearch church collection**: Many remain at local churches, with NEHGS holding many but not all transcriptions.
- **Manuscript collections at NEHGS**: Accessible only in-person or via AmericanAncestors.org subscription.

---

## Known record losses

- **King Philip's War (1675–1676):** Several towns were burned and abandoned, resulting in the loss of some local records. Towns like Deerfield, Northampton, and Springfield suffered severe damage; some early records for those communities do not survive.
- **Great Fire of Boston (1760)** and other urban fires destroyed some town and county records, though most colonial records had been moved to the Massachusetts Archives by then.
- **Plymouth Colony records:** Substantially intact and published; minimal losses.
- **General record quality variance:** Early town clerks were unpaid lay officers; recording quality varied enormously. Some births, especially of daughters and servants, were routinely omitted from early town records.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the town, not the county.** The town is the fundamental unit of record creation for this period. Know which town your ancestor lived in before searching any other record type.

2. **Plymouth Colony ≠ Massachusetts Bay Colony.** These are two separate documentary universes before 1691. Ancestors in Plymouth Colony towns (Plymouth, Duxbury, Scituate, Barnstable, etc.) will NOT appear in Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Search *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* and the FamilySearch church and vital records collections separately.

3. **The Great Migration Study (NEHGS) is a mandatory first stop** for anyone whose ancestor arrived 1620–1643. It provides family reconstructions with full source citations and English-origin research. Available at AmericanAncestors.org.

4. **Use the Vital Records of [Town] to 1850 series** (Tanner–Corbin) as a finding aid before going to original town volumes. These published abstracts cover 200+ towns and are widely available in libraries and on FamilySearch.

5. **Congregational church records are not duplicate sources — they are complementary.** Church baptism records and town birth records often contain different information or cover different children. Search both.

6. **No county existed before 1643.** Events before that date were under direct colony jurisdiction. Probate, land, and court records from 1620–1643 are found in the General Court records at the Massachusetts Archives or in published colony record volumes, not at county courthouses.

7. **Old Norfolk County (1643–c.1680) dissolved.** If your ancestor lived in towns later absorbed into Essex County or New Hampshire, determine which county actually created the relevant record before searching.

8. **King Philip's War records can prove a man's presence in a specific town** in 1675–1676. Militia muster rolls at the Massachusetts Archives are a powerful substitute when vital records are missing for that generation.

9. **The Salem Witch Trials (1692) records name hundreds of individuals**, including witnesses, accused, and family members — useful even if your ancestor was not directly involved in the proceedings.

10. **For English origins, the Great Migration Study and NEHGS manuscript collections are the primary tools.** English parish records (FamilySearch has extensive England collections) should be searched in parallel once a county of origin is identified.

11. **FamilySearch's Massachusetts Passenger Lists (1820–1891)** cover only post-colonial immigration and are irrelevant for 1620–1700 ancestors arriving in the Great Migration. Do not use that collection for this period.

12. **Statewide vital registration began in 1841, not 1639.** Town-level recording began in 1639. If you encounter a claim that "Massachusetts didn't require vital registration until 1841," that applies only to the *statewide* level — town clerks were legally required to keep vital records from 1639.

---

> **Digitization coverage note:** The four Massachusetts-specific FamilySearch Research Wiki sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned a generic fallback page rather than Massachusetts-specific content. The research tips and online-records sections above are therefore built from `wiki_search` results (sources cited inline) and the confirmed FamilySearch collections returned by `collections_search`. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy for the most current Massachusetts-specific guidance.

---

## 🗺️ Locality Research Guide: Oklahoma — Land Run Era (1889–1910)

### Jurisdictional Overview

| Fact | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Target place** | Oklahoma (present-day state) |
| **Target period** | 1889–1910 (Land Run through early statehood) |
| **FamilySearch standardPlace** | `Oklahoma, United States` |

**Critical jurisdictional split — read first:**
Oklahoma before 1907 was *two separate territories operating simultaneously*, not one:

- **Oklahoma Territory (OT)** — formally organized **May 2, 1890** under the Organic Act, covering the Unassigned Lands opened April 22, 1889, plus subsequent run areas (1891–1895). Capital: Guthrie.
- **Indian Territory (IT)** — eastern Oklahoma, governed by the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) under their own laws and courts, administered separately through the Dawes Commission.

Which jurisdiction holds a family's records depends on **exactly where they lived**. A family in Guthrie or Oklahoma City generated OT records; a family near Muskogee or Tahlequah generated IT records. Many families straddled or moved between both. Both territories merged into the **State of Oklahoma on November 16, 1907**. Never assume a single record system — search both.

County formation was rapid and fluid during the territorial period. Seven original counties were created in 1890; new counties formed continuously through 1907. Confirm which county existed at the time of the event before searching courthouse records.

---

### 🏆 Priority Records for Land Run Families

#### 1. Homestead & Land Records — **THE prime starting point**

Land Run settlers filed homestead applications at the General Land Office offices in **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher**. Each homestead file typically contains: the original application, proof of settlement (with witness names), and the final patent. **Rejected applications also survive** and often contain richer family detail than granted ones.

| Repository | What's held | Access |
|------------|-------------|--------|
| **NARA, Washington D.C.** | Homestead case files, Record Group 49 (GLO) | Physical; some digitized |
| **BLM General Land Office Records** | Land patents, searchable by name | Free online: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **FamilySearch** | "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" — 234,567 records, 117,283 images | Indexed + images, [collection 1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872) |

> **Quirk:** Sooners (those who entered before the noon gun) were disqualified — their applications were rejected and they had to refile or leave. Rejected-application files at NARA may be your only document for a family later identified as having "jumped" the run.
>
> **Quirk:** Trace where the settler *came from* — most came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas. You will need to search departure-state records to establish the family's pre-1889 history.

---

#### 2. Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|--------|----------|-------|
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** | Oklahoma Territory only (IT not included) | **One of the few surviving 1890 census substitutes nationwide** — most 1890 federal schedules were destroyed; this territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society is precious. |
| **1900 Federal Census** | All of Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory | Both territories enumerated; search under both jurisdictions |
| **1910 Federal Census** | State of Oklahoma | Post-statehood enumeration |
| **Territorial/county tax rolls (1890s)** | Oklahoma Territory counties | Oklahoma Historical Society; document early settlers between censuses |

---

#### 3. Indian Rolls & Censuses — Essential for IT families and anyone with Native ancestry

FamilySearch holds **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** — 567,890 records, 283,945 images — [collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432).

The **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)**, compiled by the Dawes Commission, are the definitive enrollment for the Five Civilized Tribes. They recorded name, age, sex, blood degree, and family relationships. Even mixed-blood and intermarried white families appear. These are at NARA and indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Freedmen (formerly enslaved persons of the tribes) were enrolled in separate Freedmen rolls.

> **Quirk:** If an ancestor lived in Indian Territory but was *not* enrolled as a tribal member, they may appear in "intruder" lists or federal court records rather than tribal rolls — check both.

---

#### 4. Vital Records

**There was no statewide vital registration until 1908** (the year after statehood). For the 1889–1907 period, births and deaths must be reconstructed from substitute sources:

- Church registers (see below)
- Family Bible records
- Census age data
- Cemetery/tombstone inscriptions
- Newspaper announcements
- Probate estate files

**Marriage records** are an exception — county clerks recorded marriages beginning with county formation in 1890:
- FamilySearch: **"Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995"** — 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images — [collection 2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789). Indexed with images.

> **Quirk:** Indian Territory marriages before statehood were governed by tribal law, not territorial law. Cherokee, Choctaw, and other tribal marriage records are held separately by the Oklahoma Historical Society and tribal archives, not in county courthouse marriage books.

---

#### 5. Church & Mission Records

Churches were established quickly as towns formed in 1889. Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian missions had already operated in Indian Territory for decades before the Land Run.

FamilySearch: **"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** — 123,456 records, 61,728 images — [collection 1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). Indexed with images.

For pre-1908 vital events, church registers are often the **only** surviving record of births and deaths. Locate the specific denomination's archives as well (e.g., American Baptist Historical Society for Baptist mission records).

---

#### 6. Territorial Court Records (1890–1907)

Oklahoma Territory district courts handled civil, criminal, probate, and **naturalization** cases. Immigrant settlers frequently naturalized in territorial courts.

| Repository | What's held |
|------------|-------------|
| **NARA at Fort Worth, TX** | Federal district court records for Oklahoma Territory |
| **Oklahoma State Archives, OKC** | Territorial and early state court records |

> **Quirk:** Indian Territory had a parallel federal court system (based in Muskogee, McAlester, and Ardmore) completely separate from Oklahoma Territory's courts. An IT family's probate or naturalization record is in the federal court records for that district, not the OT district court.

---

#### 7. Military Records

Many Land Run participants were Civil War veterans. Check:

- **NARA** — Civil War service records and pension files (huge proportion of 1889 settlers were veterans entitled to homestead preference)
- **Fold3.com** — digitized military records
- **WWI Selective Service draft cards (1917–1918)** — on FamilySearch and Ancestry; cover men born ~1873–1900, squarely overlapping the children of Land Run settlers

---

#### 8. Newspapers

Territorial newspapers began publishing in April 1889 — the *Guthrie Daily Leader* launched the day of the Land Run. They covered homestead filings, legal notices, marriages, deaths, and community news.

- **Newspapers.com** — historical Oklahoma newspapers
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — large newspaper microfilm and digital collection; [https://www.okhistory.org](https://www.okhistory.org)
- **Library of Congress Chronicling America** — some territorial-era Oklahoma papers

---

#### 9. Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — crowdsourced; many Oklahoma pioneer cemeteries indexed
- **BillionGraves** — additional coverage
- Oklahoma Historical Society maintains cemetery survey records

---

### 🏛️ Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Specialties | URL |
|------------|-------------|-----|
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)** | Territorial records, newspapers, photographs, 1890 special census, tax rolls, church records | [okhistory.org](https://www.okhistory.org) |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** | State government records, vital records (post-1908), court records | [sos.ok.gov/archives](https://www.sos.ok.gov/archives) |
| **NARA Fort Worth** | Federal court records for OT and IT, federal agency records | [archives.gov/fort-worth](https://www.archives.gov/fort-worth) |
| **NARA Washington D.C.** | GLO homestead files (RG 49), Civil War pensions, Indian Affairs (RG 75) | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |
| **BLM GLO Records** | Land patents, free name-indexed search | [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 digitized Oklahoma collections (land, Indian rolls, marriages, church records) | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, vital records, military, newspapers | [ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service records, pension files | [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Oklahoma newspapers | [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) |
| **Five Civilized Tribes archives** | Tribal rolls, IT-specific records | Individual tribal archives |

---

### ⚠️ Top Research Quirks for This Period

1. **Two territories, not one** — Always determine whether the family lived in Oklahoma Territory or Indian Territory. Records, courts, and repositories differ completely between them.
2. **1890 census gap is partially filled** — The 1890 federal census was destroyed, but the Oklahoma Territory Special Census survives at the Oklahoma Historical Society. This is rare and invaluable.
3. **No statewide vital registration until 1908** — Pre-1908 births and deaths require substitute sources (church, census, newspaper, cemetery).
4. **Trace origins in the departure state** — Most settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, or Arkansas. Exhaust those records to find the family before 1889.
5. **County boundaries were unstable 1890–1907** — A county formed after an event may have absorbed earlier records from a predecessor; confirm the county that existed at the date of the record, not at statehood.
6. **Indian Territory families → separate court system** — IT probates, naturalizations, and civil cases are in the federal court records (Muskogee, McAlester, Ardmore districts) at NARA Fort Worth, not county courthouses.
7. **Sooners' rejected homestead files** — If an ancestor's original claim was contested or rejected, that case file at NARA may be the only pre-1890 documentation you find.
