# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (ca. 1780–1819, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Around 1800, "Alabama" was not a single jurisdiction — it was a fractured colonial and territorial landscape with two concurrent governing authorities and multiple Indigenous nations controlling the interior:

| Zone | Authority ca. 1800 | Transitioned to U.S. control |
|---|---|---|
| Interior / northern Alabama | **Mississippi Territory** (est. 1798) | Remained U.S. territory; became Alabama Territory 1817 |
| Mobile Bay / Gulf Coast | **Spanish West Florida** (Mobile District, 1780–1813) | U.S. forces seized Mobile in 1813 |
| Deep interior | Creek, Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw nations | Ceded after Creek War 1813–1814 |

**Full jurisdictional sequence for the region:**
- **1702–1763** — French colonial (Fort Louis / Fort Condé at Mobile)
- **1763–1780** — British colonial (Province of West Florida)
- **1780–1813** — Spanish colonial (Mobile District, Spanish West Florida)
- **1798–1817** — Mississippi Territory (American territorial government for the interior)
- **1817–1819** — Alabama Territory
- **1819–** — State of Alabama

This dual-jurisdiction split is the defining research challenge for this period: **a family living in present-day Alabama in 1800 may have been simultaneously under Mississippi Territory administration (if inland) or Spanish crown authority (if near Mobile).** Which set of records applies depends on exactly where in the region the family lived.

*(Source: Wikipedia, "Alabama," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama; FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Before 1798:** The interior had no American civil government. Records of white settlers are rare; Indigenous nations governed themselves.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory created, encompassing present-day Mississippi and southern Alabama. Territorial civil administration begins — land offices, courts, tax lists, militia rolls.
- **1800:** Mississippi Territory expanded northward to cover most of present-day Alabama's interior.
- **1813:** U.S. forces take Mobile from Spain. Mobile District records now under American authority, but existing Spanish registers remain intact.
- **1817:** Alabama Territory carved from eastern Mississippi Territory; county-level records continue under new name.
- **1819:** Statehood. County records continue uninterrupted.

**Searcher rule:** Records for families in interior Alabama before 1817 are filed under **Mississippi Territory**, not Alabama. Records for Mobile-area families before 1813 are Spanish colonial records held in foreign archives. Search both trails for families that moved between the coast and the interior.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Alabama did **not** establish statewide civil vital registration until **1908** (state level). There is no civil birth, marriage, or death registration for this pre-statehood period.
- **County marriage records:** The earliest Alabama counties began recording marriages when they were formed — Madison County (1808), Baldwin County (1809), and a handful of others. FamilySearch holds **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images) — **indexed + images**, but coverage begins *just after* the target window.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records and territorial court records are the only substitutes for vital events before 1809. See Church Records and Court Records below.

### Church Records
- **Catholic records, Mobile area (Spanish period, 1780–1813):** The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Mobile maintained baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the Spanish era. Spanish colonial church records for the Mobile District — including census-linked sacramental registers — are held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress**. The **Mobile Municipal Archives** holds microfilm copies of the French-era registers. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)* Access: **physical or microfilm only** for the colonial originals; some finding aids online.
- **Protestant churches, interior Alabama:** Methodist and Baptist congregations formed in the Mississippi Territory period (after 1798), particularly along the Tennessee River valley. Records survival is uneven; most are held by individual congregations or state denominational archives.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — **indexed + images**. This collection begins 1803, overlapping the final years of the target window, but coverage for pre-1810 years will be sparse.

### Census Records
- **Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810):** These enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. Held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery.** *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)* Access: **physical/microfilm** — these are not in the FamilySearch indexed collections.
- **1810 Federal Census:** The first federal census to enumerate the Alabama region (as Mississippi Territory). FamilySearch holds **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, **no images** — index-only). The 1810 manuscript pages for the Alabama/Mississippi Territory area are available on Ancestry and Fold3.
- **Spanish colonial censuses (Mobile District):** Periodic enumerations of the Mobile area population under Spanish rule. Held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress**. Access: **physical only** in Seville; Library of Congress copies require on-site or mail inquiry.
- **Note:** The 1800 federal census for the Mississippi Territory (covering Alabama's interior) is damaged and incomplete. Tax lists and territorial censuses serve as the primary substitutes.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Mississippi Territory courts (1798–1817):** The first civil courts in the Alabama interior were territorial courts. Their records — wills, administrations, guardianships, civil suits — are held at ADAH and in some county courthouses.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (collection 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) — **indexed + images**. Begins 1809, covering the very end of the territorial period.
- **Mississippi collections:** FamilySearch also holds **Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920** (collection 1855293; 245,670 records, 122,835 images) — **indexed + images** — which may include records from the Alabama-portion of the Mississippi Territory for 1799–1817.

### Land Records
- **System:** Alabama is a **federal-land state** — the Public Land Survey System (rectangular survey) applies. Land patents issued by the federal government after 1803 (when land offices opened in the Mississippi Territory).
- **Spanish and British colonial land grants (Mobile area):** Spanish crown grants and British West Florida grants are the earliest land records. Held at the **Archivo General de Indias** and **British colonial archives (The National Archives, Kew)**; some transcriptions at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Mississippi Territory federal land records (1803–1817):** The federal government opened land offices in the territory after 1803. The **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM/GLO)** website (glorecords.blm.gov) has searchable patent records for Alabama, including the earliest territorial-era patents. Access: **indexed + free online** at BLM/GLO.
- **FamilySearch collection (Mississippi Territory):** **Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907** (collection 1919694; 312,450 records, 156,225 images) — **indexed + images** — covers the Mississippi Territory period and will include Alabama-area land records from 1798 to 1817.

### Military Records
- **Militia rolls, Mississippi Territory:** Territorial militia enrollment lists exist for the Alabama-area counties. Held at ADAH. Access: **physical/microfilm**.
- **Creek War (1813–1814) and War of 1812:** Service records and pension files are at **NARA** and searchable on **Fold3** (fold3.com). These are some of the richest sources for identifying men living in the Alabama region in the early territorial period.
- **Revolutionary War pension files:** Many Alabama settlers were veterans who migrated from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia. Their pension files at NARA often give birthplace, age, and residence history that carries back to the pre-Alabama period.

### Tax Records
- **Territorial tax lists (1809–):** As Alabama-area counties formed under the Mississippi Territory (1800s–1817), they began collecting taxes. These lists name heads of household and can substitute for missing census records. Held at ADAH and individual county courthouses.
- **Access:** Primarily **physical/microfilm**; some transcriptions in published genealogical compilations.

### Cemetery Records
- **Early cemeteries:** Family, church, and plantation cemeteries predate formal public cemeteries. Many survive in rural areas.
- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) has volunteer transcriptions; coverage for pre-1820 stones is uneven.
- **ADAH** has some cemetery survey records.

### Newspaper Records
- **Very sparse for this period.** The *Mobile Gazette* began publication ca. 1813 after American takeover. Interior Alabama had no local press before the territorial period stabilized. Mobile Municipal Archives and the University of South Alabama hold early issues.
- **Newspapers.com** (newspapers.com) has some Alabama holdings, but coverage before 1820 is extremely limited.

---

## Browsable / Digitized Volumes — Direct Answer to Your Question

**FamilySearch's volume_search returned zero digitized image volumes for Alabama or Mississippi Territory in the 1780–1820 window.** This is an honest gap to report: FamilySearch's film-and-scan holdings do not appear to have standalone browsable volumes covering this specific pre-statehood period in the query system. The collections that *do* exist for Alabama (marriages, probate, church records) start at 1803 or 1809 and are name-indexed rather than browse-only.

**Where browsable digitized material does exist:**
- **BLM/GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) — Federal land patent images for territorial-era Alabama, searchable and viewable free.
- **Ancestry.com** — Holds 1810 federal census images (Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory), browsable by county/township.
- **FamilySearch Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798–1907** (collection 1919694, 156,225 images) — includes Alabama-area territorial land records; images are available alongside the index.
- **FamilySearch Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes 1792–1890** (collection 1927171, 198,340 records, **index only — no images**) — index useful but no images to browse.
- **Library of Congress / Manuscripts Division** — Holds microfilm copies of Spanish colonial records from the Mobile District; some items are digitized through the LOC's digital collections portal (loc.gov), but coverage is partial and not systematically browsable as a single collection.

For unindexed browse-only scanning of early records, the best strategy is to contact **ADAH directly** — they have digitization programs and may have collections accessible through their online portal (archives.alabama.gov) that do not appear in FamilySearch's volume search.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Relevant Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama County Marriages 1809–1950; Alabama Probate Records 1809–1985; Alabama Church Records 1803–1950; Alabama Compiled Census Index 1810–1890; Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records 1798–1907; Mississippi County Court Records 1799–1920 | Free |
| BLM/GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents, Alabama territorial era | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1810 federal census images; compiled indexes | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | War of 1812 / Creek War service records; pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal land, military, pension records | Free finding aids; some digital |
| Alabama Dept of Archives & History (archives.alabama.gov) | Territorial censuses, militia rolls, tax lists, county records | Free portal; some on-site only |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept of Archives and History, Montgomery | Territorial censuses 1801–1810; militia rolls; tax lists; county records; church transcriptions | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French/Spanish-era colonial records; Mobile church registers (microfilm) | In-person |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / Atlanta) | Federal land entry files; military service and pension records; 1810–1820 census originals | In-person; microfilm; some digital |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, census returns, church registers for Mobile District | In-person; Portico portal (partial digitization) |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Microfilm copies of Spanish colonial Mobile District records | In-person; some digital via loc.gov |
| The National Archives, Kew, UK | British West Florida records (1763–1780) | In-person; some digital via Ancestry |

---

## Records NOT Online

- **Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808)** — physical/microfilm at ADAH only; not in any online indexed database.
- **Spanish colonial church registers for Mobile** — originals in Seville; microfilm copies at Mobile Municipal Archives; not indexed in any online platform.
- **French colonial records (1702–1763)** — primarily at Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **British West Florida records (1763–1780)** — primarily at The National Archives, Kew.
- **Territorial militia rolls and tax lists (1798–1817)** — at ADAH; not systematically online.
- **Individual Protestant congregation records** — scattered; most not digitized.

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1800 federal census for Mississippi Territory** — Damaged and fragmentary; the Alabama-area enumeration is largely missing. Tax lists and territorial censuses (1801, 1805) are the primary substitutes.
- **Creek War disruption (1813–1814)** — Military conflict destroyed or displaced many private and some official records in the interior. Families may have fled or relocated, leaving gaps in local record series.
- **Early Mobile courthouse records** — Some records from the Spanish-American transition period (1813–1819) are incomplete due to administrative confusion during the transfer of authority.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Always determine which jurisdiction a location was in, ca. 1800.** Coastal/Mobile-area families → Spanish colonial records. Interior families → Mississippi Territory records. The two trails are entirely separate and held in different countries.
2. **The 1810 census is your starting federal census for the Alabama interior.** The 1800 census for this region is largely lost; use territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) and tax lists as substitutes.
3. **Federal land records are often the richest pre-1820 source for interior Alabama.** The BLM/GLO database and Mississippi Territorial Land Records collection (FS collection 1919694) name heads of household in the critical 1803–1817 window.
4. **Revolutionary War pension files are frequently the best way to document families who migrated to Alabama before 1820.** Many settlers were veterans; their pension applications at NARA describe their prior residences in the Carolinas, Virginia, or Georgia.
5. **Creek War and War of 1812 service records place men in the Alabama region precisely.** If a man served in a Tennessee or Georgia militia unit called into the Alabama/Florida theater, his service record names his home county.
6. **Alabama's statewide civil vital registration began in 1908** (state level) — do not expect to find birth or death certificates for the pre-statehood period in any government registry. Church records are the sole vital-event source for this era.
7. **ADAH is the single most important repository for pre-statehood Alabama.** Before spending time on FamilySearch, check the ADAH online catalog and contact their reference staff — they hold the territorial censuses, militia rolls, and tax lists that are not online anywhere.
8. **For the Mobile area, the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception's registers are the earliest continuous record series** — Catholic baptisms, marriages, and burials going back into the Spanish period. Contact the Archdiocese of Mobile for access.

Records for Mobile-area families before 1813 are **Spanish colonial records held in foreign archives in Spain and France.**

- **County marriage records** begin with county formation: Madison County (1808), Baldwin County (1809). FamilySearch holds **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408); 612,345 records, 306,172 images) — **indexed + images** — but this barely overlaps the pre-statehood period.
- **Substitute:** Church records and territorial court records are the *only* source for vital events before 1809.

### Church Records
- **Catholic registers, Mobile area (Spanish period, 1780–1813):** The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Mobile kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the Spanish era. Originals are at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**; microfilm copies at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**; some copies at the **Library of Congress**. Access: **physical or microfilm only** — nothing in any online indexed database. Contact the Archdiocese of Mobile for access to the earliest registers.
- **Protestant churches, interior Alabama:** Methodist and Baptist congregations formed in the Mississippi Territory period (post-1798), particularly along the Tennessee River valley. Records are scattered at individual congregations or state denominational archives; survival is uneven.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396); 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — **indexed + images.** Begins 1803, covering the last portion of the target window.

Held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery.** Access: **physical/microfilm** — *not in any online indexed database.* *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*
- **1810 Federal Census:** The first federal census to enumerate the Alabama region (filed as part of Mississippi Territory). FamilySearch holds **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection [2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756); 287,634 records, **no images — index only**). The 1810 manuscript pages are viewable on Ancestry and Fold3.
- **Spanish colonial censuses (Mobile District):** Periodic enumerations under Spanish rule, held at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress. Access: **physical only.**
- **⚠️ The 1800 federal census for the Mississippi Territory is largely damaged and missing** for the Alabama area. The territorial censuses (1801, 1805) and tax lists at ADAH are the primary substitutes.

- 1763–1780: British colonial (Province of West Florida)

- 1817–1819: Alabama Territory
- 1819–: State of Alabama

- Protestant churches, interior Alabama: Methodist and Baptist congregations formed after 1798; records held by individual congregations or state denominational archives.
- FamilySearch collection: Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (collection 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — indexed + images. Begins 1803, overlapping the final years of the target window.

### Census Records
- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810): Enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. Held at Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery. Access: physical/microfilm — not in any online indexed database.
- 1810 Federal Census: First federal census to enumerate the Alabama region (as Mississippi Territory). FamilySearch: Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, no images — index only). 1810 manuscript pages available on Ancestry and Fold3.
- Spanish colonial censuses (Mobile District): Periodic enumerations under Spanish rule. Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress. Access: physical only.
- Note: The 1800 federal census for the Mississippi Territory is damaged and largely missing. Tax lists and territorial censuses (1801, 1805) are the primary substitutes.

### Probate and Court Records
- Mississippi Territory courts (1798–1817): First civil courts in the Alabama interior. Records at ADAH and county courthouses.
- FamilySearch: Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (collection 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) — indexed + images. Begins 1809.
- FamilySearch: Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (collection 1855293; 245,670 records, 122,835 images) — indexed + images — includes Alabama-area territorial records 1799–1817.

### Land Records
- System: Federal-land state; Public Land Survey System (rectangular survey).
- Spanish and British colonial land grants (Mobile area): Held at Archivo General de Indias and The National Archives, Kew; transcriptions at Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Mississippi Territory federal land records (1803–1817): BLM/GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) — indexed + images, free online.
- FamilySearch: Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (collection 1919694; 312,450 records, 156,225 images) — indexed + images — covers Alabama-area land records 1798–1817.

### Military Records
- Militia rolls, Mississippi Territory: Territorial militia enrollment at ADAH. Physical/microfilm.
- Creek War (1813–1814) and War of 1812: Service records and pension files at NARA; searchable on Fold3.
- Revolutionary War pension files: Many Alabama settlers were veterans from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia. Pension files at NARA often give prior residence history.

### Tax Records
- Territorial tax lists (1809–): As Alabama-area counties formed, they collected taxes. These lists name heads of household and substitute for missing census records. Held at ADAH and county courthouses. Primarily physical/microfilm.

### Cemetery Records
- Early family, church, and plantation cemeteries predate formal public cemeteries. FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has volunteer transcriptions; coverage for pre-1820 stones is uneven. ADAH has some cemetery survey records.

### Newspaper Records
- Very sparse. Mobile Gazette began ca. 1813. Interior Alabama had no local press before the territorial period stabilized. Mobile Municipal Archives and University of South Alabama hold early issues. Newspapers.com coverage before 1820 is extremely limited.

## Browsable / Digitized Volumes

FamilySearch's volume_search returned zero digitized image volumes for the 1780–1820 window for both Alabama and Mississippi Territory — a genuine coverage gap. The Alabama collections that exist (marriages, probate, church records) start at 1803 or 1809 and are name-indexed rather than browse-only.

Where browsable digitized material does exist:
- BLM/GLO (glorecords.blm.gov): Federal land patent images, territorial-era Alabama — free, searchable and viewable.
- Ancestry.com: 1810 federal census images (Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory), browsable by county/township.
- FamilySearch Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798–1907 (collection 1919694, 156,225 images): Images available alongside the index.
- ADAH (archives.alabama.gov): May have collections accessible through their own portal not appearing in FamilySearch volume search — contact ADAH directly.

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama County Marriages 1809–1950; Alabama Probate Records 1809–1985; Alabama Church Records 1803–1950; Alabama Compiled Census Index 1810–1890; Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records 1798–1907; Mississippi County Court Records 1799–1920 | Free |
| BLM/GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents, Alabama territorial era | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1810 federal census images; compiled indexes | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | War of 1812 / Creek War service records; pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal land, military, pension records | Free finding aids; some digital |
| ADAH (archives.alabama.gov) | Territorial censuses, militia rolls, tax lists, county records | Free portal; some on-site only |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept of Archives and History, Montgomery | Territorial censuses 1801–1810; militia rolls; tax lists; county records | In-person; some microfilmed |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French/Spanish-era colonial records; Mobile church registers (microfilm) | In-person |
| NARA (Washington D.C. / Atlanta) | Federal land entry files; military service and pension records; 1810–1820 census originals | In-person; microfilm; some digital |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, census returns, church registers for Mobile District | In-person; Portico portal (partial digitization) |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington D.C. | Microfilm copies of Spanish colonial Mobile District records | In-person; some digital via loc.gov |
| The National Archives, Kew, UK | British West Florida records (1763–1780) | In-person; some digital via Ancestry |

## Records NOT Online

- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808): physical/microfilm at ADAH only.
- Spanish colonial church registers for Mobile: originals in Seville; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- French colonial records (1702–1763): primarily at Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- British West Florida records (1763–1780): primarily at The National Archives, Kew.
- Territorial militia rolls and tax lists (1798–1817): at ADAH; not systematically online.
- Individual Protestant congregation records: scattered; most not digitized.

## Known Record Losses

- 1800 federal census for Mississippi Territory: Damaged and fragmentary; Alabama-area enumeration largely missing.
- Creek War disruption (1813–1814): Military conflict destroyed or displaced records in the interior.
- Early Mobile courthouse records: Some incomplete due to administrative confusion during the Spanish-to-American transfer of authority (1813–1819).

## Research Tips

1. Determine which jurisdiction a location was in ca. 1800. Coastal/Mobile-area families → Spanish colonial records. Interior families → Mississippi Territory records. The two trails are in entirely different countries.
2. The 1810 census is the starting federal census for the Alabama interior. For 1800, use territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) and tax lists at ADAH.
3. Federal land records are often the richest pre-1820 source for interior Alabama. BLM/GLO and FS collection 1919694 name heads of household in the 1803–1817 window.
4. Revolutionary War pension files at NARA are frequently the best way to document families who migrated to Alabama before 1820, giving prior residence in the Carolinas, Virginia, or Georgia.
5. Creek War and War of 1812 service records place men in the Alabama region precisely.
6. Alabama statewide civil vital registration began in 1908 — no civil birth or death records exist for the pre-statehood period.
7. ADAH is the single most important repository for pre-statehood Alabama. Check archives.alabama.gov and contact their reference staff before spending time on FamilySearch.
8. For the Mobile area, the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception's registers are the earliest continuous record series — contact the Archdiocese of Mobile for access.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Counties (1860–1890)
**Counties:** Schuylkill · Carbon · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Northumberland · Columbia
**Focus:** Irish immigrant mining families

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

**Schuylkill County** was formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties (county seat: Pottsville). This is the only county whose formation is confirmed by the FamilySearch place database. The other five coal counties (Carbon, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Columbia) resolved only to the state level in the place resolver — verify their individual formation dates via county histories or the Pennsylvania State Archives.

**Population (Schuylkill County, FamilySearch population data):**

| Year | Population |
|------|-----------|
| 1860 | 89,510 |
| 1870 | 116,428 |
| 1880 | 129,974 |

Growth was rapid and driven by anthracite mining. Irish, Welsh, and German immigrants dominated in the 1860s–1870s; Eastern European arrivals increased significantly from the 1880s onward.

**Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry across all six counties, powering the northeastern US industrial economy and generating record types unique to this region (payroll books, mine inspection reports, accident records).

**Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes were established between 1840 and 1870 across the coal counties to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. Registers are split between two dioceses:
- **Diocese of Scranton** — northeastern field (Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon) — covers post-1868 registers
- **Diocese of Harrisburg** — central and southern field (Schuylkill, Northumberland, Columbia) — holds pre-1868 registers for *all* six counties and ongoing coverage for the southern counties
*(Source: FamilySearch wiki, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))*

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Schuylkill:** Formed 1811; stable boundaries throughout 1860–1890.
- **Lackawanna / Luzerne split ⚠️:** The FamilySearch wiki treats the "Lackawanna Valley" as a distinct sub-region from 1855 onward, and the Diocese of Scranton was established for that area post-1868. Records for events in the northeastern anthracite field *before any county split* belong in **Luzerne County**. The precise date Lackawanna County was separated from Luzerne is not confirmed from tool output — **verify independently and search Luzerne County records for pre-split events**.
- **Other five counties:** Formation dates unconfirmed by place tools; consult Pennsylvania county histories.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
> **⚠️ No statewide civil vital registration existed in Pennsylvania during 1860–1890.** The FamilySearch collections confirm this: the Death Certificates collection begins only in 1906; County Marriages only from 1885. **Church records are the primary vital-record substitute for this entire period.**

| Collection | Coverage | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 | Post-period only — aging miners after 1906 | 4,218,763 | **Indexed + images** |
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 | Overlaps only the very end of target period | 524,189 | **Indexed + images** |

---

### Church Records ⭐ Primary Source for 1860–1890
| Source | Coverage | Volume | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985** (collection 1401638) | 1860–1890 fully covered | 1,245,830 records · 982,415 persons · 607,220 images | **Indexed + images** — free on FamilySearch |
| Schuylkill County volume (007936751) | Church Records 1842–1895 | 187 images · English & German | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | NE counties Catholic registers post-1868 | Unknown extent | Physical — contact diocese |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | All counties pre-1868; central/south counties ongoing | Unknown extent | Physical — contact diocese |

> German-language entries appear in the Schuylkill volume — the researcher must read German.

---

### Census Records
- **1860, 1870, 1880, 1900** federal censuses all cover the coal counties and are indexed.
- **The 1880 census** is the first to record each household member's *relationship to the head of household* — most valuable for proving family structure. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records))*
- **1890:** Population schedules mostly destroyed. Substitute with 1880 + 1900 + triennial tax assessments + payroll indexes.
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** Record deaths in the year preceding the census — useful for the 1860, 1870, and 1880 rounds.

---

### Naturalization Records ⭐ Critical for Irish Research
- **Pre-1906:** Scattered across county courts — Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts all had jurisdiction. Declarations of intent and petitions name the applicant's country of origin. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records))*
- **Post-September 1906:** Centralized at federal courts — NARA Philadelphia for eastern Pennsylvania.

| Volume | Coverage | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County (007936750) | Naturalization Records 1849–1915 | 298 | **Browse-only** (0% indexed) |
| Pennsylvania state (008120443) | Naturalization Records 1790–1915 | 351 | **Partially indexed** (15%) — images available |

---

### Probate Records
| Source | Coverage | Volume | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196) | Full period covered | 893,214 records · 893,214 images | **Indexed + images** |
| Schuylkill County (007936749) | Probate 1851–1930 | 412 images | **Browse-only** (0% indexed) |
| Pennsylvania state (008120441) | Probate 1683–1994 | 1,180 images | **Browse-only** (0% indexed) |

---

### Land and Deed Records
| Volume | Coverage | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County (007936752) | Deed Records 1815–1900 | 543 | **22% indexed** — partially searchable by name; images available |

Deed records name adjacent landowners and grantors/grantees, useful for establishing family relationships.

---

### Marriage Records
| Collection / Volume | Coverage | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (1571957) | Full period | 312,045 records | **Indexed + images** |
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (1921317) | End of period only | 524,189 records | **Indexed + images** |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (1502909) | Full period | 198,765 records | **Index only — no images** |
| Schuylkill County (007936753) | Marriage Records 1870–1910 | 94 images | **Browse-only** (0% indexed) |

---

### Military Records
- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Service, draft, and pension records at NARA. Irish immigrant miners served in Pennsylvania regiments. The 1863 draft records list occupation — useful for confirming miners.
- **Pennsylvania adjutant general records:** At the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### Tax Records — Pennsylvania Triennial Assessments ⭐ Intercensal Substitute
Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents **triennially from 1853**. Assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and **sometimes nativity** — the nativity field makes these records exceptionally valuable for identifying Irish immigrants. Physical at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg — not available online. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))*

---

### Coal-Industry Specific Records ⭐ Unique to This Region

These sources do not exist for ordinary US jurisdictions:

**1. Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898**
Names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Each entry includes:
- Occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver, etc.)
- Wage rate
- **Parish of origin where stated** — the key bridge to Irish civil registration

This is the most targeted finding aid for Irish immigrant miners in the northeastern anthracite field. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))*

**2. Mine Inspection and Accident Reports**
Organized by **colliery**, not by person. These confirm a miner's workplace and can cross-reference against payroll indexes to establish presence in a specific community — but they are not a name-searchable finding aid. Use payroll indexes first; use accident reports to corroborate. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records — Choosing an index](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))*

**3. Company Payroll Books**
Some survive at county historical societies. The Lackawanna Valley index was derived from such books; other fields (Schuylkill, Carbon) may have partial survivors held locally.

---

### Immigration / Passenger Records
- **Primary port for Irish immigrants:** Philadelphia; Castle Garden, New York (1855–1890) was also heavily used.
- Passenger lists record every person aboard, **including infants and young children** — examine the full manifest for all family members.
- Chain migration was intense in the coal region: neighboring households in census records often originated from the same Irish parish or townland. Neighbors are research leads.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Holdings for this region | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church & Town Records (indexed); Probate (indexed); Civil Marriages; Naturalization (partial); Deed (Schuylkill, 22%) | **Free** |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1860–1900 (indexed); Civil War service & pension records | Subscription |
| NARA Philadelphia | Post-1906 naturalization; Civil War pensions; federal court records | In-person / written request |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments 1853–1890; PA National Guard records | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | NE coal county Catholic registers post-1868 | Contact diocese |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Central/south Catholic registers; all six counties pre-1868 | Contact diocese |
| County courthouses (Pottsville, Wilkes-Barre, etc.) | Original deed books; county court naturalization records | In-person |
| County historical societies | Company payroll books; local newspapers; mine records; photographs | In-person / write |

---

## Records NOT Online

- **Catholic parish registers** beyond what FamilySearch captured — must be requested from the relevant diocese.
- **Mine inspection and accident reports** — physical at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not name-indexed.
- **Company payroll books** (except those in the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index) — held at county historical societies or lost.
- **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers, 1853–1890** — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives only.
- **Schuylkill County volumes** (probate 007936749, naturalization 007936750, church 007936751, marriage 007936753): images are on FamilySearch but every volume is 0% indexed and not full-text — plan for image-by-image browsing.
- **External links gap:** FamilySearch's curated external links for Schuylkill County returned only 2 results, both outside the 1860–1890 window. This is a gap in FS's curated list, not evidence that external resources are absent — Ancestry holds substantial Pennsylvania coal-region record sets.

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 federal census:** Population schedules almost entirely destroyed. Substitute with 1880 and 1900 censuses, Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments, and company payroll indexes.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Counties (1860–1890)

**Counties:** Schuylkill · Carbon · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Northumberland · Columbia
**Focus:** Irish immigrant mining families

## Jurisdiction overview

**Schuylkill County:** Formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties (tool-confirmed via FamilySearch place database). County seat: Pottsville.

**Carbon, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Columbia:** FamilySearch place resolver returned only state-level results for these five counties — individual county formation records are not confirmed from tool output. Consult county histories or the Pennsylvania State Archives.

**Population (Schuylkill County):** 1860: 89,510 · 1870: 116,428 · 1880: 129,974. Rapid growth driven by anthracite coal mining; large Irish, Welsh, German, and later Eastern European immigrant population.

**Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominant across all six counties.

**Ethnic composition:** Irish, Welsh, and German immigrants dominated in the 1860s–1870s; Eastern European immigrants arrived in larger numbers from the 1880s onward.

**Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes established 1840–1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrants. Diocese of Scranton (post-1868, northeastern field); Diocese of Harrisburg (central/southern field; and all six counties pre-1868).

## Boundary changes / jurisdiction quirks

- Schuylkill County: formed 1811, stable through 1860–1890.
- Lackawanna Valley / Luzerne split: The FamilySearch wiki treats the Lackawanna Valley as a distinct sub-region from 1855; the Diocese of Scranton was established post-1868 for this area. Records for events in the northeastern field before any county split should be sought in Luzerne County. Verify the exact county formation date independently.
- Other five counties: formation dates not confirmed by place tools — consult county histories.

## Available record types

### Vital records
No statewide civil registration existed in Pennsylvania during 1860–1890. The FamilySearch Death Certificates collection begins 1906; County Marriages from 1885. Church records are the primary vital record substitute for the entire period.

### Church records
- **FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985 (collection 1401638) — 1,245,830 records · 982,415 persons · 607,220 images · **indexed + images** — primary online source.
- **Schuylkill County volume** (007936751): Church Records 1842–1895 · 187 images · English/German · **0% indexed · not full-text · browse-only.**
- **Diocese of Scranton** (post-1868): northeastern coal counties — contact for Catholic registers not on FamilySearch.
- **Diocese of Harrisburg** (pre-1868 and central/southern counties ongoing): contact for Catholic registers.

### Census records
- Federal census: 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 all useful (1890 mostly destroyed).
- 1880 is the first census to record each household member's relationship to the head — most valuable for proving family structure.
- Mortality schedules 1850–1885 record deaths in the year preceding the census.

### Naturalization records
- Pre-1906: scattered across county courts (Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, Orphans' Court). Declarations and petitions name country of origin.
- Post-1906: NARA Philadelphia.
- **Schuylkill County volume** (007936750): Naturalization Records 1849–1915 · 298 images · **0% indexed · browse-only.**
- **Pennsylvania state volume** (008120443): Naturalization Records 1790–1915 · 351 images · **15% indexed · images available.**

### Probate and court records
- **FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) — 893,214 records · **indexed + images.**
- **Schuylkill County volume** (007936749): Probate Records 1851–1930 · 412 images · **browse-only.**
- **Pennsylvania state volume** (008120441): Probate Records 1683–1994 · 1,180 images · **browse-only.**

### Land and deed records
- **Schuylkill County volume** (007936752): Deed Records 1815–1900 · 543 images · **22% indexed · images available** (partially searchable).

### Marriage records
- Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957) — 312,045 records · **indexed + images.**
- Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317) — 524,189 records · **indexed + images** (overlaps only end of period).
- Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909) — 198,765 records · **index only, no images.**
- **Schuylkill County volume** (007936753): Marriage Records 1870–1910 · 94 images · **browse-only.**

### Military records
- Civil War service, draft, and pension records at NARA.
- Pennsylvania adjutant general records at Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Tax records — Pennsylvania triennial assessments
- State assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853. Lists householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. Physical at Pennsylvania State Archives — intercensal substitute and nativity finder.

### Coal-industry specific records
1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898** — ~41,000 colliery workers; occupation, wage rate, parish of origin where stated. Most targeted finding aid for Irish miners in the northeastern field.
2. **Mine inspection and accident reports** — organized by colliery, not by person; use payroll indexes first.
3. **Company payroll books** — some survive at county historical societies.

### Immigration
- Primary port for Irish immigrants: Philadelphia; also Castle Garden (New York, 1855–1890).
- Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants — examine full manifest.

## Repository guide

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church/Town Records; Probate; Civil & County Marriages; Naturalization vol. (partial); Deed (Schuylkill, 22%) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1860–1900; Civil War records | Subscription |
| NARA Philadelphia | Post-1906 naturalization; Civil War pensions; federal courts | In-person/request |
| PA State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments; PA National Guard | In-person/request |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | NE coal county Catholic registers post-1868 | Contact diocese |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Central/south Catholic registers; all pre-1868 | Contact diocese |
| County courthouses | Deed books; county court naturalizations | In-person |
| County historical societies | Company payroll books; local newspapers; mine records | In-person/write |

## Records NOT online
- Catholic parish registers beyond what is in FamilySearch Church and Town Records — request from dioceses.
- Mine inspection and accident reports — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Company payroll books (except those captured in Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index).
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers 1853–1890 — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Schuylkill County volumes for probate, naturalization, church records, and marriage: images on FamilySearch but browse-only.

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census: population schedules mostly destroyed. Substitute with 1880 and 1900 censuses, triennial tax assessments, and payroll indexes.
- 1903 records consolidation: some company payroll books were lost; survivors became the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index.

## Research tips
1. Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898) for any miner in the northeastern field — 41,000 entries with parish of origin.
2. Church records are the vital record substitute for 1860–1890 — go to the FamilySearch Church and Town Records collection first, then contact the diocesan archives.
3. The 1880 census is your most powerful census tool — first to record household relationships.
4. Pre-1906 naturalization: search county court records in the coal county where the ancestor lived. Schuylkill volume (007936750) covers 1849–1915 but is browse-only.
5. Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (from 1853): fill intercensal gaps and may record nativity — physical at State Archives, Harrisburg.
6. Search Luzerne County records for any northeastern-field event that may predate the county split; verify Lackawanna County's formation date independently.
7. Parish of origin in a payroll index or naturalization record can pivot research to Irish civil registration and church records.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, ~1749–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status during period** | "New Hampshire Grants" territory (1749–1777); Vermont Republic (independent state, 1777–1791); U.S. State from March 4, 1791 |
| **Admitted as 14th state** | March 4, 1791 |
| **Parent claimants** | New Hampshire (issued original land grants from 1749); New York (asserted competing sovereignty and issued counter-grants from ~1764) |
| **Governing body, 1777–1791** | Vermont Republic — its own constitution, General Assembly, Governor's Council, county courts, and probate districts |
| **Record level** | Primarily **town level** — Vermont is a "town records" state; vital records, land records, and most civil records were created and held at the town, not the county |
| **Population** | No population data returned by tools for this period; the 1791 state was among the most rapidly growing in New England, driven by migration up the Connecticut River valley and over the Green Mountains from Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire |
| **Economy** | Subsistence and commercial farming, potash/pearl ash production, sawmilling and gristmilling, early iron forging |
| **Ethnic composition** | Predominantly English-descent New Englanders migrating from Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire; some Scots-Irish; small Abenaki Indigenous population |
| **Religion** | Congregationalist (dominant early denomination), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist; Quaker meetings in some communities |
| **Key events** | French and Indian War skirmishes (1750s–60s); the New Hampshire/New York land grant controversy (1749–1777); Battle of Bennington and other Revolutionary War actions on Vermont soil (1777); Vermont Republic formation (1777); admission to the Union (1791) |

> **FamilySearch wiki source:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

---

## Boundary and jurisdictional complexity

This is the most critical factor for pre-statehood Vermont research, and it has three distinct phases:

### Phase 1: New Hampshire Grants (1749–1777)
Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued town charters ("grants") for the territory west of the Connecticut River beginning in 1749. New York disputed this authority and issued its own competing grants for the same land beginning ~1764, calling the region "Cumberland County" and "Gloucester County." **Records for this phase may exist in both New Hampshire state archives and New York State Archives**, as well as in surviving local town proprietors' records.

### Phase 2: Vermont Republic (1777–1791)
Vermont declared itself an independent republic on January 15, 1777, operating outside both NH and NY. It had its own constitution (the first in America to abolish adult male slavery), its own currency, its own courts, and its own land-grant system. Records created 1777–1791 belong to Vermont Republic institutions — primarily town clerks, county courts, and probate districts.

**Original Vermont Republic counties** (relevant to the late 1700s):
- Bennington County (formed 1778 — oldest)
- Windham County (1779)
- Windsor County (1781)
- Rutland County (1781)
- Orange County (1781)
- Addison County (1785)
- Chittenden County (1787)
- Caledonia, Essex, Franklin, Grand Isle, Lamoille, Orleans, Washington counties — formed after 1791; their pre-formation records are held by the parent county

### Phase 3: U.S. State (from March 4, 1791)
Federal records begin (1790 federal census captured Vermont, which had just been admitted). State infrastructure built on the existing republic's county and town framework.

> **Quirk:** If your ancestor's county was not yet formed when the event occurred, search the parent county. Caledonia (1792), Washington (1810), Franklin (1792), Orleans (1792), Essex (1792), Grand Isle (1802), and Lamoille (1835) all postdate statehood; their late-1700s records sit in Chittenden, Orange, or other parent counties.

---

## Available record types

### 1. Land records ⭐ *Most important for the pre-statehood period*

**FamilySearch wiki documents the following directly:**

> *"The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."*
> — FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

This is your primary substitute for missing vital and census records in the pre-1791 period.

**Other land record types for this period:**
- **Town proprietors' records** — Each granted town had a body of proprietors (original grantees). Proprietors' meetings and land division records were maintained at the town level. Many survive; some are digitized at FamilySearch or Ancestry; others remain in manuscript at town clerk offices or the Vermont State Archives.
- **Town land records (grantor/grantee deed books)** — Vermont land transfers are recorded at the town clerk's office (not the county recorder as in most states). Town deed books for many Vermont towns begin in the 1760s–1780s. The Vermont State Archives and FamilySearch have microfilmed many of these.
- **New Hampshire colonial grants** — The original Wentworth grants naming proprietors survive at the New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) and in published form (*New Hampshire Provincial and State Papers*, vols. 24–26, available in major research libraries).
- **New York competing grants** — For researchers whose ancestor held a NY-issued grant, records are at the New York State Archives (Albany) under Cumberland County and Gloucester County records.
- **Vermont Public Land Records** — Land grants issued by the Vermont Republic (1777–1791) and early state are held by the Vermont State Archives. The Vermont Land Records Online project (at the individual town level) digitizes deed books; coverage varies by town.

**Access:** Town clerk offices hold the original deed books. The Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) holds many copies and some originals. FamilySearch has microfilmed Vermont land records for most towns — search the FamilySearch Catalog by town name to identify what's filmed. Online digitization varies by town.

---

### 2. Vital records

**FamilySearch wiki states directly:**

> *"Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857. Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly."*
> — FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

**Practical meaning for the late 1700s:**
- **No civil vital registration requirement** existed during the pre-statehood period or the early state period. The 1857 statewide mandate came 66 years after statehood.
- **Town-level recording** was practiced by some town clerks, at their discretion, from the 1770s forward — but survival and completeness are highly uneven. One town may have near-complete birth records from 1780; the neighboring town may have nothing before 1820.
- **Access:** Contact individual town clerk offices directly. The Vermont Vital Records database maintained by the Vermont State Archives collects what has been submitted; FamilySearch has indexed some pre-1870 Vermont vital records. Check the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific town.

**Pre-registration alternatives (critical for this period):**
- **Church records** (see below) — baptisms, marriages, burials are the primary substitute
- **Family Bibles** — commonly held by the Vermont Genealogical Society or deposited at the Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT)
- **Town histories** — see below
- **Cemetery inscriptions** — headstone dates and family groupings
- **Probate records** — name family members and sometimes give ages

---

### 3. Church records

Church records are among the richest sources for events not captured by town clerks in this period.

**Denominations present and record types:**
- **Congregationalist** (dominant): Baptism, marriage, and burial registers; membership records; disciplinary proceedings. Many Vermont Congregationalist churches were gathered in the 1760s–1790s. Records held at local churches, the Congregational Library & Archives (Boston, MA), and some are microfilmed at FamilySearch.
- **Baptist**: Multiple Baptist churches formed 1780s onward. Records at local churches and the American Baptist Historical Society. Some FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Presbyterian**: Small but present, especially in areas settled from New York. Records at the Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia, PA).
- **Methodist**: Circuit riders active from the late 1780s; formal church records more common post-1800.
- **Quaker**: Monthly meeting records at the New England Yearly Meeting archives (Providence, RI) and the Rhode Island Historical Society. Some Vermont meetings operated in the 1780s.

**Gaps:** Many early Vermont churches did not maintain systematic registers, and records held only in local custody are at risk of loss or inaccessibility. When a church no longer exists, its records may have transferred to a successor church, the Vermont Historical Society, or a denominational archive — check all three.

---

### 4. Census records

| Record | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1790 Federal Census** | Vermont statewide | Vermont was admitted March 4, 1791, but was enumerated in 1790 — this is the **first federal census including Vermont**. Lists heads of household only; ticks for free white males (by age bracket), free white females, all other free persons, and slaves. Indexed + images available on Ancestry and FamilySearch (free). |
| **Pre-1790 enumerations** | None identified by tools | No Vermont Republic territorial census is known. The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (see Land Records) is the closest pre-statehood listing. |
| **Tax/rate lists as substitutes** | Town level | Some Vermont towns assessed polls and property rates in the 1780s; these lists act as census substitutes and may survive in town clerk records or the Vermont State Archives. |
| **Continental Army/militia musters** | 1775–1783 | Muster rolls and pay abstracts list men by name; held at NARA (RG 93) and the Vermont State Archives. |

> **Note:** The 1800 federal census is the second census capturing Vermont and provides the first family-unit picture after statehood. For children born in the 1770s–1780s, the 1800 and 1810 censuses may help triangulate birth years.

---

### 5. Probate records

Vermont probate was organized at the **county level** under the Vermont Republic from 1778 onward, predating statehood. The probate districts followed county lines.

- **Record types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardian bonds, dower releases, distribution decrees
- **Start dates:** Some probate records survive from the late 1770s for the original counties (Bennington, Windham, Windsor, Rutland, Orange)
- **Where held:** Vermont Probate Court records are housed at the Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) for older records; current probate courts also hold some originals. FamilySearch has microfilmed Vermont probate records; check the FamilySearch Catalog by county.
- **Value for this period:** Inventories often list names of heirs, creditors, and guardians — filling in family structure when vital records are absent. Pre-1800 inventories can document household goods, farm animals, tools, and land parcels in remarkable detail.

> **Quirk:** For counties formed after 1791, pre-formation probate records sit under the parent county. Confirm county formation dates before deciding where to search.

---

### 6. Military records

The pre-statehood period coincides squarely with the Revolutionary War.

- **Green Mountain Boys / Vermont militia:** The Green Mountain Boys (Ethan Allen's force) and the Vermont militia generated muster rolls, pay vouchers, and pension applications. Vermont militia records are held at the Vermont State Archives and have been partially published.
- **Continental Army service:** Vermont men who served in Continental regiments appear in NARA Record Group 93 (Revolutionary War service records). These are microfilmed and indexed; images available on Fold3 (subscription) and some on FamilySearch.
- **Pension files:** Revolutionary War pension and bounty land warrant application files at NARA (M804) are among the richest genealogical sources for this period. They often contain age, birthplace, names of family members, and migration history. Available indexed + images on Fold3 and Ancestry; FamilySearch has partial coverage.
- **Battle of Bennington participants (August 1777):** Casualty and participant lists have been published and are available through the Vermont Historical Society.
- **Loyalist records:** Vermont had a Loyalist minority; some fled to Canada (Quebec, Ontario). If an ancestor disappears from Vermont records in the 1776–1783 window, check Upper Canada and Quebec records for Loyalist land grants.

**Access:** NARA (Washington, D.C. / St. Louis); Vermont State Archives; Fold3 (subscription); FamilySearch (free, partial).

---

### 7. Town histories

**FamilySearch wiki states directly:**

> *"Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."*
> — FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

Vermont has an exceptionally rich tradition of 19th-century town histories, many of which transcribe proprietors' records, early vital records, family genealogies, and lists of first settlers. These are:
- **Often the only surviving source** for pre-1800 events in a given town
- Held at the Vermont Historical Society (Barre), town libraries, and in digitized form at Google Books, HathiTrust, and the Internet Archive
- Searchable by town name in the FamilySearch Catalog and WorldCat

---

### 8. Probate/court records (general civil courts)

Vermont Republic courts were established by 1778. County courts of record, superior courts, and the Vermont Supreme Court all produced records — civil suits, criminal proceedings, name changes, and pre-1906 naturalizations could appear in any court of record.

- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (Montpelier)
- **FamilySearch microfilm:** Many county court records have been filmed; search the FamilySearch Catalog by county

---

### 9. Cemetery records

- Early Vermont cemeteries (family plots, church burial grounds, town cemeteries) were established from the 1760s onward
- Headstone inscriptions are often the only documentation of death date and family relationships for this period
- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com — free) and **BillionGraves** have indexed many Vermont cemeteries; coverage is volunteer-driven and uneven for very early stones
- The **Vermont Old Cemetery Association** (VOCA) has conducted physical surveys of many early cemeteries; their records are held at the Vermont Historical Society
- Some early gravestone inscriptions were transcribed by the DAR; check the DAR Genealogical Research System

---

### 10. Newspapers

Vermont's earliest newspapers date from the pre-statehood period:
- *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington, 1781–1800s) — one of the first Vermont newspapers; carries legal notices, land sales, death notices
- *Vermont Journal* (Windsor, 1783–) — early Windsor County coverage
- Content value: legal notices, land sales, tavern licenses, estate notices, marriage announcements (sparse for this early period)

**Access:** Newspapers.com (subscription), the Vermont Digital Newspaper Project (Chronicling America / Library of Congress — free), and the Vermont Historical Society newspaper collections.

---

### 11. Immigration/emigration

Vermont in the late 1700s was a **destination**, not a port of arrival. The relevant migration for this period is:

- **Internal migration from southern New England** (Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island) — traceable through town vital records and land records in those origin states
- **Migration to/from Canada** — Border crossing was fluid; some families moved north into Quebec and Ontario (especially Loyalists post-1783); some French Canadians moved south. Quebec Catholic parish records (PRDH database) are the source on the Canadian side.
- **Formal immigration records** are generally not applicable for this period and population

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | What to expect for Vermont pre-1791 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Microfilmed Vermont town vital records (partial, pre-1870), county probate records, county court records, early land records by town; 1790 federal census; Revolutionary War service records (partial) | Free |
| **Ancestry** (ancestry.com) | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); Revolutionary War pension files (Fold3 partner); some Vermont vital records transcriptions; DAR lineage papers | Subscription |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Revolutionary War NARA records — service records (M881), pension files (M804), bounty land warrants; indexed + images | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Vermont newspapers digitized from 1781 onward | Subscription |
| **Chronicling America** (loc.gov/chroniclingamerica) | Vermont Digital Newspaper Project — selected early Vermont papers | Free |
| **HathiTrust / Internet Archive / Google Books** | Vermont town histories, published proprietors' records, published genealogies | Free |
| **New Hampshire Provincial and State Papers** (digitized) | Original Wentworth grant records naming Vermont township proprietors | Free (HathiTrust) |
| **Vermont Land Records Online** (vcgi.vermont.gov) | Town deed books — coverage varies by town; many towns have early deed books available | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings relevant to pre-1791 Vermont | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Vermont State Archives** (Montpelier, VT) | Vermont Republic and early state records: county court records, probate records, early vital records submitted by towns, military records (VT militia/Green Mountain Boys), public land records, legislative records | In-person; some records by request |
| **Vermont Historical Society** (Barre, VT) | Town histories, family Bibles, genealogical manuscripts, newspaper collections, Vermont Old Cemetery Association surveys, DAR transcriptions | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **Town clerk offices** (each Vermont town) | Original vital records (some from 1760s–70s onward), deed books, proprietors' records, town meeting minutes | In-person or written inquiry |
| **New Hampshire State Archives** (Concord, NH) | Original Wentworth grant records for the New Hampshire Grants territory; NH colonial court records that may reference pre-1777 Vermont settlers | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **New York State Archives** (Albany, NY) | Cumberland County and Gloucester County records (NY's colonial-era claim over Vermont): NY-issued land grants, some court records | In-person |
| **National Archives** (NARA, Washington, D.C.) | Revolutionary War service records (RG 93), pension files (M804), 1790 census original schedules | In-person; many microfilmed and digitized |
| **Congregational Library & Archives** (Boston, MA) | Congregationalist church records from Vermont, 1760s onward | In-person; some records filmed |
| **New England Yearly Meeting Archives** (Providence, RI) | Quaker meeting records, including Vermont | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types for pre-statehood Vermont are known to exist but are **not available in any online database** — a researcher cannot assume these do not exist simply because an online search returns nothing:

- **Town proprietors' records** held only in original town clerk custody (not filmed or digitized for many towns)
- **Early town clerk vital records** before ~1800 for many towns — some filmed by FamilySearch but a significant portion remains in town offices only
- **Vermont Republic legislative and executive records** (Vermont State Archives, Montpelier — in-person only)
- **Most Vermont church registers** from the 1760s–1800s — Congregationalist, Baptist, and Methodist records held at local churches or denominational archives, not digitized
- **Vermont militia pay vouchers and muster rolls** beyond what has been published — Vermont State Archives
- **County court civil case files** (as opposed to docket books) — Vermont State Archives
- **Town rate/tax lists** from the 1780s — many exist in town clerk custody but have not been microfilmed or indexed

---

## Known record losses

- **No major statewide courthouse disaster** is documented for Vermont comparable to the Virginia courthouse-fire problem. Vermont's decentralized town-level record-keeping actually helped: because records were not concentrated in a single county courthouse, losses from individual fires were localized.
- **Individual town losses** do occur — some early town records were lost to fire, flood, or neglect. When a town's records are silent for the early period, check the Vermont Historical Society for whether that town's records are known to be deficient.
- **New York/New Hampshire jurisdictional period losses** — Records created under NY or NH authority during the disputed period (pre-1777) may have been disrupted or never formally transferred. Some NH grant-period records exist only in published form or in archives outside Vermont.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the 1790 federal census.** Vermont was enumerated in 1790 — this is your first systematic federal listing of Vermont households. It captures the generation that was of working age during the pre-statehood period. Available indexed + images on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry.

2. **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is your pre-1791 "census."** As documented by the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, this is the earliest systematic resident list for the territory — ~1,800 grantees named with their grant details. If your ancestor is not found here, they may have arrived after 1771 or held no proprietary interest in town land. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

3. **Town histories are primary sources, not just background.** As the FamilySearch wiki documents, Vermont's 19th-century town histories (published 1860–1900) routinely reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise inaccessible. Search HathiTrust, Internet Archive, and Google Books for the history of the specific town. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

4. **Vermont records at the town level, not the county.** Unlike most U.S. states, Vermont vital records and land records were created and held at the **town clerk's office**. Do not search only by county — identify the exact town and go there.

5. **Check both NH and NY archives for the pre-1777 period.** If your ancestor was a settler before 1777, records may exist in New Hampshire (Wentworth grant records) or New York (Cumberland/Gloucester County records) rather than in Vermont at all.

6. **Revolutionary War records are rich for this generation.** Nearly every adult male in Vermont in the late 1700s had some connection to the war. NARA pension files (M804) are the single richest genealogical source — they frequently give birthplace, age, family members' names, and migration history in the veteran's own words.

7. **Follow the family south.** Vermont settlers came predominantly from Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire. If Vermont records are thin, trace the family in their origin state — births and marriages often appear in MA or CT town records before the migration. Conversely, some families moved on to New York, Ohio, or Upper Canada after 1791.

8. **New Hampshire/New York border counties on both sides.** Families near the Connecticut River also generated records in New Hampshire. Families near the Lake Champlain corridor may appear in Clinton, Essex, or Franklin County, New York records. Search both sides of each border.

9. **Use probate records as a vital-record substitute.** Vermont Republic probate districts were operating by the late 1770s. An estate inventory names heirs, relationships, and sometimes birth information — essential when no town vital record exists.

10. **FamilySearch Catalog search by town.** Go to FamilySearch.org → Search → Catalog and search by the specific Vermont town name. The catalog lists every collection FamilySearch has microfilmed or digitized for that town, which is far more precise than a record search alone.

---
